teile.einleitung: The simple present is the simple present tense in English. You need it for habits, regular actions and things that are always true.
wichtigste: The simple present describes habits and general facts.
With he, she and it you add an -s: she plays.
After -ch, -sh, -s, -x and -o you add -es: watches, goes.
Consonant plus y becomes -ies: flies.
Negatives use don't or doesn't.
Signal words are usually, always, often, every day.

abschnitte.text: The **simple present** is used for things you do regularly: “She goes to school every day.” It is also used for **general facts**: “The sun rises in the east.” What is happening at this very moment, on the other hand, is expressed with the present progressive, for example “I am reading”.

With **he, she and it** the verb gets an -s: “He plays football.” If the verb ends in -ch, -sh, -s, -x or -o, you add **-es**: “watches”, “goes”. If it ends in a consonant plus y, the y becomes i: “fly” becomes “flies”. The verb “have” is irregular: “Tom has a dog.”

With I, you, we and they the negative uses **don't**: “They don't like spinach.” With he, she and it you use **doesn't**. The -s then moves to “does”, and the verb is in its basic form: “He doesn't play football.”

Certain words show that the simple present is right. They include **always**, **usually**, **often**, **sometimes** and **never**. “Every day” or “on Mondays” are also typical. These frequency words usually come before the verb: “I usually walk to school.”

gewusst: Questions in the simple present are formed with “do” or “does”: “Do you like pizza?”
The -s with he, she and it is one of the most common mistakes when learning English.

teile.einleitung: A short circuit happens when electricity takes a very short path without passing through anything that uses it. Then a very large current flows, and wires and batteries can become dangerously hot.
wichtigste: In a short circuit, the positive and negative terminals are connected directly.
The current flows without passing through a lamp, motor or other device.
Because there is hardly any resistance, the current becomes very large.
Wires and batteries can get hot, melt or burn.
Fuses switch off the electricity automatically in a short circuit.

abschnitte.text: In a normal **circuit**, the current flows from the battery through a **device**, for example a small bulb, and back again. The device slows the current down; it has a **resistance**. If you connect the two terminals directly with a wire, this brake is missing. Then a huge amount of current flows all at once. The energy turns into heat, and the wire and the battery get hot.

A short circuit can make cables melt and start a **fire**. Rechargeable batteries in mobile phones or bike lights can also get very hot. That is why you should never put batteries loose in your pocket with keys or coins. Damaged cables where the insulation is missing are dangerous too. Much more current flows from a socket than from a battery, so you must never tinker with one yourself.

Every house has a **fuse box**. It contains fuses that switch off immediately if there is too much current. This protects cables and appliances from overheating. After a short circuit, you first have to unplug the faulty appliance. Only then do you switch the fuse back on.

gewusst: Some old fuses contain a thin wire that is designed to melt through if there is too much current.

teile.einleitung: When interpreting art, you try to find out what a work of art means. You look closely, describe what you see and then ask which story, symbols and thoughts lie behind it. Many old pictures are full of hidden signs that you can decode like a puzzle.
wichtigste: Interpreting art means working out the meaning of a work of art.
Erwin Panofsky developed a model with three stages: description, iconographic analysis and iconological interpretation.
Iconography identifies the content and motifs of pictures, for example saints by their attributes.
In Christian art the apostle Peter is usually shown with a key.
Vanitas still lifes with a skull, candle or hourglass remind you that everything passes.
In Holbein’s painting “The Ambassadors” from 1533 a distorted skull is hidden, an anamorphosis.
Aerial perspective makes distant things look further away through bluer and paler colours.

abschnitte.text: When **interpreting art**, you ask: what can be seen, how is it made and what is it meant to mean? To do this you look at motifs, colours, light, composition and the time when the work was made. It is important to look closely and to back up your interpretation with observations. Often there is not just one right answer, but several **interpretations**.

The art historian **Erwin Panofsky** developed a model with three stages. First you describe what you see, for example a man with a key; this is the pre-iconographic description. Then you identify the subject, that is, that it is the apostle Peter; this is the **iconographic analysis**. Finally the **iconological interpretation** asks what the picture reveals about the thinking and beliefs of its time.

In Christian art you recognise saints by their **attributes**, that is, by objects given to them. Peter carries a key, Paul a sword, and Saint George fights a dragon. In **vanitas still lifes**, skulls, snuffed-out candles, hourglasses or wilting flowers remind you that life does not last. In old pictures a dog often stands for loyalty.

Jan van Eyck’s **“Arnolfini Portrait”** from 1434 shows a couple in a room with many details, such as a round convex mirror and a little dog. In the mirror you can see two more people, perhaps the painter himself. In **“The Ambassadors”** by Hans Holbein the Younger from 1533 there is a distorted patch on the floor. Only when you look at it from the side do you recognise a skull, a so-called **anamorphosis**.

The design of a picture is also important for interpreting it. A **triptych** is a picture in three parts, often an altarpiece with a central panel and two wings. A **repoussoir** is a motif in the foreground, for example a tree or a figure at the edge of the picture, that leads the eye into the depth. With aerial perspective, mountains in the distance look paler and bluer, just as in real life.

At school you often learn to **describe a picture** in steps: first impression, description, analysis and interpretation. Museums such as the Kunstmuseum Basel, which owns a large Holbein collection, offer guided tours for children. Holbein himself worked in Basel for some years before he went to England. With a little practice you discover new secrets in every picture.

begriffe.erklaerung: The study of the content of pictures and their symbols.
An object by which you recognise a figure, for example a key for Peter.
Latin for transience, the theme of many still lifes.
A distorted picture that only looks right from a certain angle.
A work of art in three parts, often an altarpiece.

gewusst: Above the mirror in the “Arnolfini Portrait” it says in Latin: “Jan van Eyck was here 1434”.
The skull in Holbein’s “Ambassadors” was perhaps meant to be suddenly recognised as you left the room.
The two masterpieces “Arnolfini Portrait” and “The Ambassadors” both hang in the National Gallery in London.

teile.einleitung: Iconography is the study of the content and symbols of pictures in art. It helps you recognise who is shown in a picture and what certain things mean.
wichtigste: Iconography explains what figures and symbols in pictures mean.
You can often recognise saints by their attributes, that is, typical objects.
In Christian art a white dove represents the Holy Spirit.
Saint Catherine of Alexandria can be recognised by a wheel.
Saint George is shown as a dragon slayer.

abschnitte.text: The word **iconography** comes from Greek and means something like “describing images”. In the past many people could not read. Pictures in churches told them stories from the Bible and about saints. So that people could recognise the figures, they were given fixed **attributes**. An attribute is a typical object or animal that belongs to a person.

In Christian art a **white dove** stands for the **Holy Spirit**. According to the Gospels, the Spirit of God came down like a dove at the **baptism of Jesus**. Since then the Holy Spirit has often been painted as a dove. You often see it above Jesus or in rays of light.

Saint **Catherine of Alexandria** can be recognised by a **wheel**. According to legend she was to be tortured on a spiked wheel, but the wheel broke. Saint **George** is usually shown as a knight on horseback with a lance. According to legend he defeated a **dragon** and so saved a town. The apostle **Peter** often holds a key in his hand.

The four **evangelists** also have their own symbols. Matthew is recognised by a man or angel, Mark by a **lion**. Luke has an **ox** and John an **eagle**. You find these symbols in many old churches and books. Mark’s lion, for example, is the heraldic animal of Venice.

gewusst: Iconography exists not only in Christian art, but also for the gods of ancient times and in other religions.
With iconography you can often find out who is shown in old paintings, even without names.

teile.einleitung: Artists are people who create works of art, for example pictures, sculptures, photos, installations or street art. They show us the world through different eyes and make us marvel, laugh or think. Switzerland, too, has produced many world-famous artists.
wichtigste: Artists create works such as pictures, sculptures, installations or street art.
Vincent van Gogh came from the Netherlands, Frida Kahlo from Mexico.
The sculptor Alberto Giacometti from the Grisons is known for very thin, elongated figures.
Ferdinand Hodler painted the “Woodcutter” and mountains such as the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau.
Jean Tinguely built moving machine sculptures such as the Carnival Fountain in Basel.
In 1936 Meret Oppenheim covered a cup, saucer and spoon with fur.
Banksy is an anonymous British street artist who works with stencils.

abschnitte.text: An **artist** creates works that express something or make you think. There are painters, sculptors, photographers, illustrators and people who work with video or light. Many study at an **art school**, for example at the Zurich University of the Arts. Some become famous during their lifetime, others only after their death.

**Vincent van Gogh** from the Netherlands painted sunflowers and starry nights with strong brushstrokes, but hardly sold any pictures during his lifetime. The Mexican **Frida Kahlo** became famous for colourful self-portraits in which she also showed her pain after a serious accident. The Austrian Gustav Klimt painted pictures with lots of gold leaf, such as “The Kiss”. The anonymous Briton **Banksy** sprays funny and critical pictures on house walls using stencils.

**Alberto Giacometti** came from the Bregaglia valley in the Grisons and created very thin, elongated bronze figures. His sculpture “L’Homme qui marche I” is one of the most expensive works of art ever sold at auction. **Ferdinand Hodler** painted the “Woodcutter”, pictures from Swiss history and mountains such as the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau. Albert Anker from Ins in the canton of Bern often painted children and village life.

abschnitte.titel: Tinguely and Niki de Saint Phalle
abschnitte.text: **Jean Tinguely** built machine sculptures out of scrap metal that move, clatter and squeak. His **Carnival Fountain** from 1977 stands in front of the Theater Basel, and the Museum Tinguely in Basel shows many of his works. His wife **Niki de Saint Phalle** created the Nanas, large, colourful and cheerful female figures. Her “Guardian Angel” has been floating in the main hall of Zurich main station since 1997.

In 1936 **Meret Oppenheim** covered a cup, saucer and spoon with fur and so became a well-known artist of Surrealism. The work is now in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Sophie Taeuber-Arp from Davos was a pioneer of **abstract art** and belonged to the circle of Dadaists in Zurich. Paul Klee, born near Bern, created his own poetic visual language.

Switzerland honours some artists by showing them on **banknotes**. The notes of the eighth series showed, for example, Le Corbusier, Sophie Taeuber-Arp and Alberto Giacometti. An early 50-franc note showed a woodcutter after Ferdinand Hodler. The banknotes of today’s ninth series, on the other hand, show themes such as time, light or water.

begriffe.erklaerung: A three-dimensional work of art, for example of stone, wood or bronze.
Art in public spaces, for example on house walls.
A cut-out template through which you spray paint.
An art movement that shows dreamlike and puzzling things.

gewusst: After a serious bus accident, Frida Kahlo began painting in bed, with a mirror above her.
Vincent van Gogh painted about 900 paintings in only around ten years.
In 2018 one of Banksy’s pictures shredded itself right after it was sold at auction, thanks to a built-in shredder.

teile.einleitung: The Kuleshov effect shows how film editing changes the meaning of a picture. The same face looks sad, hungry or thoughtful, depending on which picture is shown before or after it.
wichtigste: The effect is named after the Soviet director **Lev Kuleshov**.
Kuleshov carried out his experiments around 1920 in Moscow.
He combined the same expressionless face with different pictures.
The audience interpreted the facial expression differently depending on the picture.
Only **montage**, that is putting the pictures together, creates the meaning.

abschnitte.text: Kuleshov took a shot of an actor with a calm, expressionless face. He edited this shot together with different pictures, for example with a bowl of soup or a coffin. The viewers were shown each version. Many thought that the actor was showing hunger one time and grief another. Yet the face was always exactly the same.

In film, joining individual shots together is called **editing** or **montage**. Our brain automatically looks for a connection between two pictures that come one after the other. In this way a little story forms in our head. The Kuleshov effect shows that this story depends a great deal on the editing. So a single **shot** often has no fixed meaning.

Kuleshov taught at a film school in Moscow and influenced other well-known directors. Film-makers all over the world use the effect deliberately, in feature films, advertising and videos. In the news and on social media, too, editing can influence how we understand something. So it is worth asking when watching videos: do these pictures really belong together?

gewusst: The director Alfred Hitchcock explained the effect in an interview using shots of his own face.

teile.einleitung: Johannes Itten was a Swiss painter, art teacher and colour theorist. He taught at the famous Bauhaus and wrote a colour theory that is still used in many schools today.
wichtigste: Johannes Itten was born in 1888 in the canton of Bern and died in Zurich in 1967.
He was first a primary school teacher and then became a painter.
From 1919 to 1923 he taught at the Bauhaus in Weimar.
There he led the preliminary course that all students began with.
In his book “The Art of Color” he describes seven colour contrasts.
His twelve-part colour wheel is still widely used today.

abschnitte.text: Itten grew up in the Bernese Oberland and trained as a **teacher** in Bern. After that he studied painting, among other places in Stuttgart with the painter Adolf Hölzel, who was very interested in colour. Itten painted pictures himself, often with strong colours and clear shapes. But he became most important as an **art educator**, that is, someone who shows how to learn and teach art.

The **Bauhaus** was an art school in Germany that combined art, craft and design. Itten was one of the first teachers and led the **preliminary course**. There the students practised with materials, shapes, colours and rhythm before specialising in one subject. Later Itten founded his own schools and in Zurich ran the School of Applied Arts and the Museum of Applied Arts.

A **contrast** is a clear difference that catches the eye. Itten distinguished seven: the contrast of hue, the **light-dark contrast**, the **cold-warm contrast**, the **complementary contrast**, the simultaneous contrast, the contrast of saturation and the contrast of extension. In the cold-warm contrast, for example, blue looks cool and orange warm. These contrasts can explain why a picture looks calm or exciting.

Itten’s **colour wheel** has twelve sections. In the middle are the three primary colours yellow, red and blue. From them you mix the secondary colours orange, violet and green, and then six more in-between shades. Colours that are opposite each other on the wheel are **complementary colours**. This wheel is still used today in art lessons at many Swiss schools.

gewusst: Itten’s book “The Art of Color” came out in 1961, long after his time at the Bauhaus.
Itten was not only a painter, he also shaped generations of art teachers.

teile.einleitung: Painting is the art of putting pictures onto a surface with colours, for example onto canvas, paper, wood or a wall. It is one of the oldest arts of humankind and began in the caves of the Stone Age. People still paint portraits, landscapes, still lifes or completely abstract pictures today.
wichtigste: Painting is creating pictures with colours on a surface.
Many painters paint with oil paint on a canvas that stands on an easel.
Painters mix their colours on the palette.
A painted picture of a person is called a portrait; if the artist paints themselves, it is a self-portrait.
A still life shows fruit, flowers or objects; a landscape shows mountains, meadows and lakes.
The oldest paintings are cave pictures from the Stone Age.
Ferdinand Hodler is a well-known Swiss painter who painted mountains and a woodcutter.

abschnitte.text: **Painting** means putting paint on a surface with a brush, palette knife or fingers. Depending on the paint, we distinguish, for example, oil painting, **watercolour**, acrylic painting and tempera. Wall painting on damp plaster is called fresco. Painting can show reality, or express feelings only with colours and shapes.

Many painters put their picture on an **easel**, a wooden stand, while they work. Oil paintings are usually painted on a **canvas** stretched over a wooden frame. Painters mix their colours on the **palette**, a board with a hole for the thumb. They also need brushes of different sizes, rags and often a palette knife.

A painted picture of a person is called a **portrait**; if an artist paints themselves, it is a self-portrait. A **still life** shows fruit, flowers or objects on a table. Landscape pictures show mountains, meadows, lakes or the sea. History paintings tell stories from religion, legends or history; genre paintings show scenes from everyday life.

The oldest known paintings are pictures of animals in caves such as Chauvet and Lascaux in France; they are many tens of thousands of years old. The ancient Egyptians and Romans painted tombs and walls. In the 15th century Jan van Eyck refined **oil painting**, which allowed glowing colours and fine details. Since the 20th century there has also been abstract painting, which no longer shows objects.

Around 1900 **Ferdinand Hodler** painted the Swiss mountains, the “Woodcutter” and large pictures from history. Albert Anker showed children and village life in the canton of Bern. **Giovanni Segantini** painted the mountain world and the life of farmers in the Engadine; his Alpine Triptych can be seen in the Segantini Museum in St Moritz. Cuno Amiet and Giovanni Giacometti brought glowing colours into Swiss painting.

You do not need much to paint: paper, a brush, water and a paint box are enough. With the three primary colours red, yellow and blue you can mix many other colours. Professionals often first make a **sketch** in pencil before they apply paint. The important thing is to look closely and try out new things.

begriffe.erklaerung: A stand on which a picture rests while it is being painted.
A board on which painters mix their colours.
A picture painted with transparent water-based paints.
A picture of things that do not move, such as fruit, flowers or vessels.
Fabric stretched over a frame and used as a surface for painting.

gewusst: The cave pictures of Chauvet in France are about 36,000 years old.
In the past painters had to mix their paints themselves from pigment powder and oil; paint tubes have only existed since the 19th century.
Ferdinand Hodler’s “Woodcutter” was also pictured on an old Swiss banknote.

teile.einleitung: Weihnachten is called “Christmas” in English. England has its own customs, which are different from those in Switzerland.
wichtigste: “Christmas” means Weihnachten.
The gift-bringer is called “Santa Claus” or “Father Christmas”.
Children in England unwrap their presents on the morning of 25 December.
Children hang up a stocking.
26 December is called “Boxing Day”.
People wish each other “Merry Christmas”.

abschnitte.text: **Christmas** is the Christian festival of the birth of Jesus Christ. That is why the word “Christ” is in it. People wish each other **Merry Christmas**, because “merry” means cheerful. The Weihnachtsbaum is called a “Christmas tree”.

The gift-bringer is called **Santa Claus**. In England he is also called **Father Christmas**. He brings the presents during the night. In Switzerland, on the other hand, it is usually the Christkind (Christ Child) who brings the presents, and the Samichlaus (St Nicholas) comes earlier, on 6 December.

Before Christmas children in England hang up a big sock, a **stocking**. It often hangs on the fireplace or on the bed. During the night it is filled with little presents. On the morning of **25 December** the children unwrap their presents. In Switzerland this usually happens on the evening of 24 December.

In England 26 December is called **Boxing Day** and is a public holiday. The name has nothing to do with the sport of boxing. It comes from “box”. In the past, servants, for example, received a box of presents on this day.

gewusst: A typical English Christmas dinner is turkey, often followed by “Christmas pudding”.
At Christmas dinner many families pull “Christmas crackers”, paper tubes that open with a bang.

teile.einleitung: Crochet is a kind of handicraft in which you use a single needle with a hook to form stitches from a thread. In this way you can make hats, blankets, little animals and much more.
wichtigste: For crochet you only need one needle with a hook.
There is always only one loop on the hook.
A piece of crochet usually starts with a chain of chain stitches.
Important stitches are the chain stitch, the double crochet and the treble crochet.
A treble begins with a yarn over and is taller than a double crochet.

abschnitte.text: For crochet you only need **one needle**. At the front it has a small **hook** that you use to catch the thread. Unlike knitting, there is always only **one loop** on the hook. Crochet hooks come in different thicknesses. For thick wool you use a thick hook, for fine yarn a thin one.

A piece of crochet usually starts with a **chain of chain stitches**. To make it, you pull the thread through the loop on the hook again and again. This makes a chain of the width you want. You then crochet the **first row** into this chain. Row by row, the work grows.

The **double crochet** is short and makes a dense fabric. For a **treble**, you first wrap the thread once around the hook; this is called a **yarn over**. Then you insert the hook and finish the stitch. This makes the treble taller than a double crochet. Many patterns can be combined from these basic stitches.

gewusst: Small crocheted figures and animals are called amigurumi; the word comes from Japan.
You can sew crocheted squares together to make a big, colourful blanket.

teile.einleitung: Plain weave is the simplest way of crossing threads to make a woven fabric. The crosswise thread always goes alternately over one and under one lengthwise thread. This makes a very strong fabric.
wichtigste: Plain weave is the simplest and strongest kind of weave.
The crosswise thread goes alternately over one and under one lengthwise thread.
In the next row it is exactly the other way round.
Both sides of the fabric look the same.
Together with twill and satin, it is one of the three basic weaves.

abschnitte.text: In weaving, you first stretch lots of threads lengthwise; these are the **warp threads**. Then you pass a thread across through them, the **weft thread**. In plain weave it goes over one warp thread, under the next, over again and so on. In the next row it starts the other way round. This creates a pattern like a tiny **chessboard**.

Because the threads cross at every step, they hold each other very firmly. That is why plain weave is **especially strong** and hardly slips. The front and back look the same. Many fabrics for shirts, blouses, bed linen and bags are woven this way. The **canvas** for paintings also has this weave, which is where its German name comes from.

You can easily try out plain weave. You cut parallel slits in a sheet of paper and weave coloured paper strips alternately over and under. It works in exactly the same way with wool on a small **weaving frame** made of cardboard. Depending on the type of fabric, this weave is also called cloth weave or taffeta weave.

gewusst: Plain weave is the oldest known kind of weave and was used thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: “Some” and “any” both mean roughly “a few” or “a bit of”. Which word you use depends on whether a sentence is positive, negative or a question.
wichtigste: “Some” is used in positive sentences.
“Any” is used mostly in negative sentences and questions.
In requests and offers you use “some”, even in questions.
Both go with countable and uncountable nouns.
Compounds: something, anything, somewhere, anywhere.

abschnitte.text: In positive sentences you use **some**: “There are some apples on the table.” This fits countable things such as apples. But it also fits things you cannot count, such as water or milk: “There is some milk in the fridge.”

In ordinary questions and in negative sentences you use **any**: “Have you got any brothers or sisters?” or “There isn't any milk in the fridge.” Because “isn't” is already negative, you must not add “no” as well.

An important exception: in **requests** and **offers** you use “some”, even though it may be a question. Examples: “Would you like some cake?” or “I'd like some water, please.” Here you expect the answer “yes”.

Some and any form new words. **Something** means a particular thing you do not name, **anything** means any thing at all. **Somewhere** and **anywhere** are about places. With a negative, anywhere means “in no place”: “I can't find it anywhere.”

gewusst: “Much” only goes with uncountable things such as water, “many” only with countable ones such as apples. “Some” and “any” go with both.

teile.einleitung: Max Bill was a Swiss artist, architect and designer. He is seen as one of the most important figures of concrete art. As the first rector of the Ulm School of Design, he shaped modern design.
wichtigste: Max Bill was born in Winterthur in 1908 and died in 1994.
He studied at the **Bauhaus** in Dessau.
He was a leading figure of **concrete art**.
He designed the buildings of the Ulm School of Design and was its first rector until 1956.
He also designed furniture, clocks, posters and typefaces.
For some years he was a member of the National Council.

abschnitte.text: Max Bill grew up in Winterthur and first trained as a silversmith in Zurich. Then he studied at the **Bauhaus** in Dessau, a famous school of art and design. There he learned to combine art, craft and technology. Later he lived and worked mainly in Zurich. He was a painter, sculptor, architect and graphic designer all at once.

Bill was an important figure of **concrete art**. This art does not copy anything from nature, but shows only colours, areas and shapes. It is often based on mathematical rules. Together with other artists such as Richard Paul Lohse, he belonged to the **Zurich Concretists**. His sculptures in the shape of an endless loop are also well known.

In the 1950s Max Bill helped to found a new school in Ulm: the **Ulm School of Design**. He designed its buildings and was its first rector until 1956. The school wanted to build on the ideas of the Bauhaus. Here students learned to design everyday objects that were both beautiful and practical. The Ulm School influenced design all over the world.

Bill designed many things that people use in everyday life. His simple **watches and clocks** for the company Junghans are well known. Together with Hans Gugelot he designed the **Ulm stool**, which can be a seat, a little table and a shelf all at once. He also designed posters, books and exhibitions. For him, good design should be simple, clear and useful.

gewusst: Max Bill was a member of the Swiss National Council from 1967 to 1971.
His wristwatches for Junghans are still made today almost unchanged.

teile.einleitung: A light-emitting diode, LED for short, is a small electronic component that gives off light. LEDs use little electricity and last a very long time. You find them in lamps, screens, bike lights and many devices.
wichtigste: LED is short for “Light Emitting Diode”.
An LED only lights up when the current flows in the right direction.
The longer leg is the **anode** and goes to the positive terminal.
The shorter leg is the **cathode** and goes to the negative terminal.
An LED usually needs a **series resistor** that limits the current.
LEDs use much less energy than old light bulbs.

abschnitte.text: A **diode** is a component that lets current through in one direction only. You can think of it as a valve. A light-emitting diode is a special diode made of a **semiconductor**. When current flows through it in the right direction, it gives off light. Depending on the material, it glows red, green, blue or another colour.

An LED has two legs. The **longer leg** is the anode and is connected to plus. The shorter leg is the cathode and goes to minus. Often the casing is also flattened on the cathode side. If you connect the LED the wrong way round, it simply does not light up.

An LED can only take a little current. Without protection, a 9-volt battery would send far too much current through it, and the LED would be **destroyed**. That is why you put a **series resistor** in front of it. It limits the current to a safe value. Which resistor is right depends on the battery and the LED and can be calculated.

An LED turns much more electricity into light than a **light bulb**, which mainly produces heat. It also lasts for many years. That is why most old light bulbs were gradually taken off the market in Switzerland and Europe. White LED light is often produced by a blue LED with a yellowish **phosphor layer**. The invention of the bright blue LED won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014.

gewusst: The first LEDs only glowed a faint red and were used mainly as small indicator lights.
A screen can be made of millions of tiny points of light that work with LED technology.

teile.einleitung: Contrapposto is a pose of figures in sculpture and painting. One leg carries the weight, the other is relaxed. This makes the figure look natural and lively.
wichtigste: In contrapposto there is a **supporting leg** and a **free leg**.
The supporting leg carries the weight, the free leg is relaxed.
The hips and shoulders tilt in opposite directions.
This makes the figure look full of movement and lively instead of stiff.
Contrapposto began in ancient Greece.
It was taken up again in the Renaissance, for example in Michelangelo’s David.

abschnitte.text: The word **contrapposto** comes from Italian and means something like counter-position. The figure stands on one leg, the **supporting leg**. The other leg, the **free leg**, is slightly bent and only touches the ground lightly. On the side of the supporting leg the hip is higher. The shoulder on this side, however, drops a little.

Early Greek statues stood very stiff and straight, with both feet firmly on the ground. In the 5th century BC sculptors began to spread the weight unevenly. A famous example is the **Spear Bearer** by the sculptor **Polykleitos**. The Romans took over the pose and made many copies of Greek works.

In the Middle Ages contrapposto was not common. In the **Renaissance**, artists in Italy studied the ancient statues closely again. Michelangelo’s **David** in Florence is a well-known example of contrapposto. Since then the pose has been part of the basic knowledge taught in art schools. You also often see it in drawings and photos of people.

Stand up straight and then shift your weight onto one leg. You notice how your hip rises and your shoulders tilt slightly. Your body forms a gentle **S-curve**. It is exactly this curve that makes a figure in works of art look alive. When drawing, it helps to put in the slanting lines of the shoulders and hips first.

gewusst: Most people stand in contrapposto quite naturally in everyday life, for example when waiting at the bus stop.
Many famous Greek statues are only known from Roman marble copies.

teile.einleitung: The United States of America, USA for short, is one of the largest countries in the world. It consists of 50 states and stretches from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
wichtigste: The USA consists of 50 states and the capital district of Washington, D.C.
In 1776 the colonies declared their independence from Great Britain.
Alaska is the largest state by area.
Hawaii is a chain of islands in the Pacific and became the 50th state in 1959.
California has the most inhabitants.
The main language is English, the currency the US dollar.

abschnitte.text: Thirteen colonies on the east coast of North America used to belong to Great Britain. In 1776 they declared themselves independent. **Thomas Jefferson** wrote most of the **Declaration of Independence**. That is why 4 July is still the national holiday today, “Independence Day”. The first president was George Washington.

The USA is a **federal state**, similar to Switzerland with its cantons. Each of the **50 states** has its own laws and its own government. In addition there is the capital district of **Washington, D.C.**, where the president works in the White House. The last two states, Alaska and Hawaii, joined in 1959.

**Alaska** lies in the north-west of North America next to Canada. It is by far the largest state, more than twice the size of Texas. The USA bought Alaska from Russia in 1867. **Hawaii** lies in the middle of the Pacific Ocean and consists of a chain of islands with volcanoes.

**California** on the west coast is the state with the most people, with around 39 million inhabitants in 2025. That is more than four times as many people as in the whole of Switzerland. In second place comes Texas. The largest city in the USA is New York.

gewusst: The 50 stars on the flag stand for the 50 states, the 13 stripes for the first 13 colonies.
At federal level the USA has no official language laid down by law, but English is by far the most important language.

teile.einleitung: A 3D printer builds objects up layer by layer. In this way a computer model becomes real parts, for example figures, spare parts or models. Today 3D printers are found in factories, workshops and many schools.
wichtigste: 3D printing is an additive process: material is added layer by layer.
In the widespread FDM process a plastic thread is melted and laid down.
Stereolithography hardens liquid resin with UV light.
In selective laser sintering a laser fuses plastic or metal powder.
Models are often saved as an STL file, which describes the surface with triangles.
A slicer cuts the model into layers and produces the G-code for the printer.

abschnitte.titel: Building up instead of cutting away
abschnitte.text: 3D printing is a form of **additive manufacturing**. Additive means building up: the part is made from many thin layers laid on top of each other. In **milling** or **turning** it is the other way round. There, material is removed from a block; these are called **subtractive processes**. The advantage of 3D printing: even complicated shapes with hollow spaces can be made.

The most common is **FDM**, which stands for Fused Deposition Modeling. A hot nozzle melts a plastic thread, the **filament**, and lays it down track by track. In **stereolithography**, UV light hardens a liquid resin layer by layer. Chuck Hull patented this process in 1986. In **selective laser sintering**, a laser fuses fine powder, and the loose powder supports the part.

First you draw a model on the computer. It is often saved as an **STL file**, which breaks the surface down into many small triangles. Then a program, the **slicer**, calculates the individual layers, the infill pattern and any supports needed. From this the **G-code** is produced, a list of commands that the printer works through step by step.

A popular filament is **PLA**, polylactic acid. It is usually made from plant starch, for example from **maize** or **sugar cane**. PLA is easy to print and hardly smells. However, it is only biodegradable in industrial composting plants, not simply in the garden or in nature.

For a long time 3D printers were expensive and found only in industry. From 2005 **Adrian Bowyer** at the University of Bath developed the open project **RepRap**. The idea: a printer that can print many of its own parts. The plans were freely available. This made cheap machines possible, which today are found in classrooms too.

gewusst: The name RepRap comes from “replicating rapid prototyper”, a machine meant to build copies of itself.
With laser sintering it is even possible to print parts made of metal.

teile.einleitung: Copper is a shiny, reddish metal. It conducts electricity and heat very well and is therefore used for cables, pipes and many other things. Copper also plays a part in art.
wichtigste: Copper is a chemical element with the symbol Cu.
After silver, copper is the best conductor of electricity.
Because it is much cheaper than silver, most cables are made of copper.
In the air, copper slowly gets a green layer, the patina.
Bronze is a mixture of copper and tin, brass a mixture of copper and zinc.
Copper is easy to recycle.

abschnitte.text: In a metal, tiny particles called **electrons** can move easily. That is why electricity flows through it well. After silver, copper is the **best electrical conductor**. So there is almost always copper wire in power cables, charging cables and motors. Copper also conducts heat very well and is used for pans and heating pipes.

Copper is one of the first metals that people worked. Some of it was even found pure in nature. Later people mixed copper with tin and got **bronze**, which is harder. The **Bronze Age** is named after this material. The Latin name “cuprum” is a reminder of the island of Cyprus, where a lot of copper was mined in ancient times.

New copper shines reddish. Over time it reacts with air and water and turns first brown, then green. This layer is called **patina** and protects the metal underneath. That is why many church towers and old roofs are green. The Statue of Liberty in New York is also made of copper and is therefore green.

Copper is soft enough to bend, hammer and engrave. In **copper engraving**, an artist cuts a picture into a copper plate. The grooves are filled with ink and printed onto paper. Bowls, jewellery and figures are also made from copper sheet. Bells and many statues are made of bronze, that is, mainly of copper.

gewusst: Copper is one of the few metals that do not look silvery or grey.
Old copper is valuable and is collected, because it can be melted down again and again without losing quality.

teile.einleitung: The Baroque is a period of art, architecture and music that lasted from about 1600 to 1750. Typical features are splendour, movement, strong feelings and dramatic effects of light. From Rome to Einsiedeln, magnificent churches and palaces were built.
wichtigste: The Baroque lasted from about 1600 to 1750.
Baroque art is splendid, full of movement and full of feeling.
Caravaggio became famous for strong contrasts of light and dark.
Rembrandt painted “The Night Watch” in 1642, Diego Velázquez “Las Meninas” in 1656.
Louis XIV had the Palace of Versailles magnificently extended.
Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed the colonnades of St Peter's Square in Rome.
Johann Sebastian Bach is seen as one of the most important composers of the Baroque.

abschnitte.text: The word **Baroque** probably comes from the Portuguese “barroco”, an irregularly shaped pearl. At first it was meant disapprovingly, because people found the art overdone. The period began around 1600 in Italy and spread across the whole of Europe. Churches and princes wanted to show their power and their faith through splendour.

The Italian Caravaggio painted with very strong **contrasts of light and dark**, known as chiaroscuro. The Flemish painter Peter Paul Rubens from Antwerp is known for powerful figures full of movement. The Dutch painter Rembrandt created the large group portrait “The Night Watch” in 1642. The Spanish court painter Diego Velázquez painted “Las Meninas” in 1656, one of the most puzzling pictures in the history of art.

Baroque buildings have curved façades, domes and lots of gold and stucco. In Rome **Gian Lorenzo Bernini** designed the mighty colonnades that embrace St Peter's Square. In France Louis XIV had the Palace of Versailles extended with the Hall of Mirrors and huge gardens. Afterwards many princes in Europe built similar palaces.

In Switzerland Baroque art developed mainly in Catholic areas. The abbey church of **Einsiedeln** in the canton of Schwyz was built from 1719 to 1735 to plans by Caspar Moosbrugger. The Asam brothers decorated its interior with magnificent paintings and stucco. St Gallen Cathedral is also a famous Baroque building, and the Abbey of St Gall is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Music also flourished in the Baroque period. **Johann Sebastian Bach** wrote cantatas, organ works and the Brandenburg Concertos. George Frideric Handel composed operas and the oratorio “Messiah”, Antonio Vivaldi “The Four Seasons”. The first operas were also written at this time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A longer stretch of time with shared features.
A way of painting with strong contrasts of light and dark.
Plaster decorations on ceilings and walls.
A large musical work for choir, soloists and orchestra, often with religious content.

gewusst: “The Night Watch” is actually set in the daytime; it only looked so dark because the varnish had darkened.
In 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.
After his death Bach's music was almost forgotten and only became famous again through Felix Mendelssohn in 1829.

t1b90w7f.t: Days of the week in English

teile.einleitung: A week has seven days, “seven days” in English. Here you learn the English names of the days of the week and how to write them.
wichtigste: Montag is “Monday”, Dienstag “Tuesday”.
Mittwoch is “Wednesday”, Donnerstag “Thursday”.
Freitag is “Friday”, Samstag “Saturday”, Sonntag “Sunday”.
In English the days of the week always have a capital letter.
Monday contains “moon”, Sunday “sun”.

abschnitte.text: **Monday** is Montag; it contains “moon”. **Tuesday** is Dienstag, pronounced roughly like “tjusdei” in German spelling. **Wednesday** is Mittwoch: it is written with a d, but you hardly pronounce it. **Thursday** is Donnerstag and **Friday** Freitag.
**Saturday** is Samstag. On Saturdays there is usually no school. **Sunday** is Sonntag; it contains “sun”. Saturday and Sunday together are called the “weekend”.

In English most words are written with a small letter. But the days of the week are **always written with a capital letter**, even in the middle of a sentence: “I play football on Monday.” Before a day of the week comes the word **on**: “on Friday”.

gewusst: Many English days of the week are named after old Germanic gods, for example Thursday after the thunder god Thor, as is the German Donnerstag.
Saturday is named after the Roman god Saturn.

teile.einleitung: Watercolour painting is a painting technique using transparent water-based paints. The paint is applied to paper with lots of water. This makes watercolours look light, bright and glowing.
wichtigste: Watercolour paints are transparent: the paper shines through.
White areas are made by leaving the paper unpainted.
You usually paint from light to dark.
In wet-on-wet painting the colours run softly into each other.
In glazing you lay thin layers of paint on top of each other.
Watercolour paper is thick and absorbent.
Unlike watercolour, gouache is opaque.

abschnitte.text: Watercolour paints consist of finely ground **pigments** and a binder, usually **gum arabic**. Thinned with water, they form a very thin layer of paint. This layer is **transparent**: the light paper shimmers through and makes the colours glow. The German name “Aquarell” comes from the Latin word **aqua**, water.

In classic watercolour painting you do **not paint white**. The lightest areas are made by **leaving the paper bare**. That is why you plan in advance where the highlights and light areas will go. Because you cannot paint light over dark, you work **from light to dark**: first the delicate tones, the dark ones last.

In the **wet-on-wet** technique you first dampen the paper or paint into an area of paint that is still wet. The colours **flow into each other** and form soft transitions. This is good for skies, clouds, water and fog. You cannot fully control how the paint spreads, and that is exactly what makes it appealing.

In **glazing** you wait until a layer of paint is dry and then paint another thin layer over it. Because both are transparent, the colours mix **optically** on the paper. Blue over yellow, for example, looks green. This creates depth and fine gradations.

For watercolours you need **thick, absorbent paper**. It hardly cockles with lots of water; thin paper would warp or tear. A related water-based paint is **gouache**. It contains more pigment and filler and is therefore **opaque**. With it you can paint light colours over dark ones too.

gewusst: The English painter William Turner became famous for his glowing watercolours of light and sky.
As early as around 1500 Albrecht Dürer painted landscapes and animals with watercolours.

teile.einleitung: Architecture is the art of planning and constructing buildings. It combines technology, beauty and usefulness, from the Greek temple to the modern stadium. Good architecture shapes how we live, work and feel in a city.
wichtigste: Architecture comes from the Greek word for “master builder”.
The Greek orders of columns are Doric, Ionic and Corinthian.
The Parthenon in Athens was dedicated to the goddess Athena.
Cologne Cathedral is a famous Gothic building.
Filippo Brunelleschi built the great dome of Florence Cathedral.
The Bauhaus was founded in Weimar in 1919.
Swiss architects such as Le Corbusier and Herzog & de Meuron are world-famous.

abschnitte.text: The ancient Greeks built temples with columns in fixed forms, the **orders of columns**. You can recognise the Corinthian column by its capital with acanthus leaves. The most famous temple is the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens, which was built for the goddess Athena in the 5th century BC. The Romans also invented concrete and built domes, as in the Pantheon.

In the Middle Ages, from the 12th century onwards, **Gothic** architecture developed, with pointed arches and huge windows. Cologne Cathedral was begun in 1248 and only completed in 1880. Typical features are stained-glass windows and the rose window, a large round window with stone tracery. The churches were meant to seem tall and bright, like an image of heaven.

In the Renaissance, builders took up the forms of antiquity again. In Florence Filippo Brunelleschi built the enormous dome of the cathedral, which was consecrated in 1436. In Barcelona **Antoni Gaudí** created the Sagrada Família church with shapes that recall plants and stalactites. Building began in 1882 and has already lasted well over a hundred years.

In 1919 Walter Gropius founded the **Bauhaus** in Weimar, a school for art, craft and architecture. Modernism relied on clear shapes, concrete, steel and glass. An important figure was Le Corbusier, whose real name was Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, born in La Chaux-de-Fonds in 1887. He designed houses, churches and even whole districts of cities.

The Basel firm **Herzog & de Meuron** designed the National Stadium in Beijing for the 2008 Olympic Games, known as the “Bird's Nest”. The Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg is also by them. Peter Zumthor built the thermal baths in Vals from slabs of gneiss. Mario Botta from Ticino is known for buildings made of striped stone.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fixed rules for the shape of columns in antiquity.
The decorated top part of a column.
A large round window in Gothic churches.
A curved roof in the shape of half a sphere.

gewusst: After its completion in 1880, Cologne Cathedral was for a few years the tallest building in the world.
Le Corbusier is pictured on the former Swiss 10-franc note.
Brunelleschi's cathedral dome in Florence was built without a fixed wooden framework rising from the ground.

teile.einleitung: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec was a French painter and graphic artist. He showed the nightlife in the Paris district of Montmartre and turned the advertising poster into an art form.
wichtigste: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec lived from 1864 to 1901.
He came from Albi in the south of France.
He painted and drew life in the Paris district of Montmartre.
In 1891 he created his first famous poster for the Moulin Rouge.
The poster shows the dancer La Goulue.

abschnitte.text: **Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec** was born in 1864 in **Albi** in the south of France. He came from a noble family. As a teenager he broke both legs, and afterwards they did not grow properly any more. That is why he stayed short. He moved to **Paris** and became a painter there. He died as early as 1901, aged 36.

In 1891 Toulouse-Lautrec created a poster for the **Moulin Rouge**, a famous Paris entertainment venue with dancing and music. The poster shows the dancer **La Goulue** with flat colours and bold outlines. It was quite different from the usual posters of the time. It made the artist famous overnight.

Toulouse-Lautrec printed his posters using **lithography**, a printing process with stone plates. He used large areas of a single colour and clear lines. He was also inspired by **Japanese colour woodblock prints**. In this way he turned the **advertising poster** into an art form of its own. Many later graphic artists were inspired by him.

gewusst: In his home town of Albi there is a museum just for his works.
In his short life Toulouse-Lautrec created thousands of drawings and pictures.

teile.einleitung: Cultural history explores how people in earlier times lived, thought, believed and created things. It is not only about kings and wars, but about art, religion, books, customs, food and everyday life. In this way you understand why our world today is the way it is.
wichtigste: Cultural history studies the thinking, art, knowledge and everyday life of people in the past.
In 1860 the Basel historian Jacob Burckhardt wrote “The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy”.
Johannes Gutenberg’s printing with movable type around 1450 fundamentally changed how knowledge spread.
In 1516 Erasmus of Rotterdam published the Greek New Testament in Basel.
From 1519 Huldrych Zwingli worked at the Grossmünster in Zurich and shaped the Reformation.
The Enlightenment demanded that people use their own reason.
The Convent of St John in Müstair is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and has wall paintings from around 800.

abschnitte.text: **Cultural history** is a part of the study of history. It asks, for example, how people lived, what they ate, which books they read and what they believed in. To find out, it studies works of art, letters, tools, clothes and buildings as **sources**. The Basel historian **Jacob Burckhardt**, with his book “The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy” from 1860, is seen as one of its most important founders.

In the Middle Ages, monasteries were important places for learning, books and art. The **Convent of St John in Müstair** in the Val Müstair has wall paintings from the Carolingian period around 800 and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983. The Abbey Library of St Gallen also keeps precious manuscripts from this time. In 1919 the Dutchman Johan Huizinga described the feeling of life at the end of this era in the book “The Autumn of the Middle Ages”.

Around 1450 **Johannes Gutenberg** in Mainz invented printing with movable type. Books could now be made much faster and more cheaply, and knowledge spread rapidly. Basel became an important printing city, where in 1516 the humanist **Erasmus of Rotterdam** published the Greek New Testament. Humanists wanted to rediscover the knowledge of ancient times.

From 1519 **Huldrych Zwingli** preached as people’s priest at the Grossmünster in Zurich and called for a renewal of the Church. The **Reformation** changed faith, worship, school and everyday life in many parts of Europe. Later John Calvin worked in Geneva. Because of the Reformation, Switzerland split into Reformed and Catholic areas.

In the 18th century Immanuel Kant described the **Enlightenment** as “mankind’s emergence from its self-incurred immaturity”. People were to think for themselves instead of simply believing everything. Around 1770, on the other hand, the **Sturm und Drang** (Storm and Stress) movement stressed feeling, nature and genius, for example in the young Goethe and in Schiller. In 1939 the sociologist Norbert Elias showed how people in Europe learned to control their feelings and table manners more and more.

Cultural history helps you understand where our festivals, words, habits and ideas come from. It shows that many things that seem obvious to us were once new, for example forks, compulsory schooling or newspapers. Today it also studies **digitalisation** as a great upheaval, similar to printing in its day. Museums, archives and libraries keep the most important sources for this.

begriffe.erklaerung: An old piece of evidence such as a letter, picture or tool from which you learn something about the past.
A movement that stressed the knowledge of ancient times and the value of human beings.
Renewal of the Church in the 16th century, out of which the Reformed churches arose.
An era in the 18th century that stressed reason and thinking for yourself.

gewusst: Jacob Burckhardt was pictured on the 1,000-franc note of the eighth series.
Erasmus of Rotterdam died in Basel in 1536 and is buried in Basel Minster.
In 1938 Johan Huizinga also wrote the book “Homo Ludens” about the importance of play for culture.

teile.einleitung: The Leica is a German camera that went on sale from 1925. It was small and light and made the 24 x 36 millimetre format famous. In doing so it changed photography a great deal.
wichtigste: The name Leica stands for “Leitz Camera”.
The camera comes from the company Ernst Leitz in Wetzlar in Germany.
The engineer Oskar Barnack designed it for 35 mm cinema film.
From 1925 the Leica was sold in series.
It made the **35 mm format** of 24 x 36 mm the standard.
Photojournalists could now take spontaneous photos on the street.

abschnitte.text: In the past cameras were big and heavy. You often needed a **tripod** and glass plates or large films. **Oskar Barnack** wanted to build a handy camera. For this he used **35 mm film**, which was actually meant for cinema films. The result was a camera that you could put in your coat pocket.

A picture on the Leica’s film is **24 by 36 millimetres**. This is called the **35 mm format**. Lots of pictures fitted on one film one after another. Other makers took over the format, and it became the standard for decades. With today’s digital cameras, too, people still speak of the full-frame or 35 mm format when the sensor is this size.

With the light Leica, photographers could move about freely. They photographed people in the street, at work or at events, often without being noticed. This is how **street photography** and modern **photojournalism** developed. Many famous photos of the 20th century were taken with a Leica. The Frenchman Henri Cartier-Bresson is a well-known example.

gewusst: The camera that Barnack first built for himself is now called the “Ur-Leica”, the original Leica.
Photos on 35 mm film were often shown as slides, that is, projected onto a wall.

teile.einleitung: A house or flat has many rooms, and each room has its own name in English. If you know these words, you can talk in English about where you live and what you do at home.
wichtigste: The English word “room” means Zimmer or Raum.
The Küche is called the “kitchen”, the Badezimmer the “bathroom”.
The Schlafzimmer is called the “bedroom”, the Wohnzimmer the “living room”.
The Esszimmer is called the “dining room”.
The Garten is called the “garden”, the Treppe the “stairs”.
The Tür is called the “door”, the Wand the “wall” and the Boden the “floor”.

abschnitte.text: Many English names for rooms are made of two words. The second part is often **room**. “Bed” means Bett, which is why the **bedroom** is the room where you sleep. “Bath” means Bad, which is why the **bathroom** is the room with the bath or shower. If you know the building blocks, you can guess many words yourself.

In the **kitchen** people cook. Watch out: “chicken” is the hen and “kitten” the young cat, and they sound similar. People often eat in the **dining room**. “To dine” means to eat a meal. In many flats the kitchen and dining room are a single room.

In the **living room** the family sits together, reads, plays or watches television. “To live” means to dwell or to be alive. People sleep in the **bedroom**. In the **bathroom** you wash, brush your teeth and have a shower. A child's room can be called a “children's room” or simply “my room”.

You go up to the upper floor by the **stairs**. That is why “upstairs” means on the upper floor and “downstairs” on the lower one. You go in and out through the **door**. A room has four **walls**, a **floor** and above, a ceiling, the “ceiling”. Light comes in through the **window**.

The **garden** is the Garten; the word sounds almost like German. The Dach is called the **roof**. Under the house there is often a cellar, “cellar” or “basement” in English. A small Balkon is called a “balcony” in English. That way you can name the whole house from bottom to top.

gewusst: “Upstairs” and “downstairs” both come from the word “stairs”.
“Kitchen”, “chicken” and “kitten” are often mixed up, although they mean Küche, Huhn and Kätzchen.
In American English the garden behind the house is often called the “backyard”.

teile.einleitung: The waste hierarchy is a ranking of the best ways to deal with waste. At the top is avoiding it, at the bottom disposing of it. The higher up a measure is, the better it is for the environment.
wichtigste: First comes: avoid waste.
Next come reuse and recycling.
Only then comes burning, which often still produces energy.
Last of all comes dumping in a landfill.
Switzerland follows the principle: avoid, reduce, recover.
Many municipalities charge a fee per rubbish bag so that less waste is produced.

abschnitte.text: The best waste is the waste that is never produced. **Avoiding** means, for example, using a drinking bottle instead of disposable cups, shopping with your own bag or buying only as much as you need. Anyone who throws away less saves raw materials, energy and often money too.

If waste cannot be avoided, **reusing** is the next best solution. A jar becomes a storage pot, and clothes are passed on. After that comes **recycling**: old materials are made into new products. In Switzerland, for example, **PET bottles**, glass, aluminium, paper and cardboard are collected separately.

In Switzerland, what cannot be recovered usually goes to a **waste incineration plant**. The heat produced there is used to generate electricity or to heat houses. Since the year 2000, combustible waste may no longer be dumped in **landfills** in Switzerland. Landfills mainly take leftovers that do not burn, for example slag from incineration.

In many municipalities people pay a **bag fee** for every rubbish bag. Behind this is the **polluter-pays principle**: whoever produces more waste pays more. This is meant to encourage people to avoid waste and to collect recyclable materials separately. The rules are set out in the federal Environmental Protection Act, and the municipalities and cantons organise the collection.

gewusst: The European Union has also laid down a waste hierarchy with five stages.
New bottles can be made again from collected PET bottles.

teile.einleitung: Aerial perspective is a technique in painting for showing depth. Things in the distance are painted lighter, paler and bluer. This makes a flat picture look as if you could see far into the landscape.
wichtigste: In nature, distant things look lighter, paler and bluer.
The reason is the air, which scatters the light.
Blue light is scattered more strongly in the air than red light.
As distance increases, contrasts and details decrease.
Leonardo da Vinci described and used aerial perspective.
It is also called atmospheric perspective.

abschnitte.text: If you look at the Alps on a clear day, you can see this for yourself. The nearby hills are dark green and sharp. The mountains behind them look bluish, and the furthest peaks are almost only pale blue. The further away something is, the **paler** it looks and the **less contrast** it has. In the distance you can hardly make out small details any more.

There is a lot of air between our eye and a mountain. Tiny particles such as water droplets and dust float in it. They **scatter the light**, that is, they send it off in all directions. Blue light is scattered more strongly than red light. That is why a light, bluish veil settles over distant things. In haze or fog this effect is especially strong.

Painters use this observation to show **depth**. They paint the foreground strong, dark and precise. They paint the background lighter, cooler and less sharp. **Leonardo da Vinci** wrote about this effect and used it in his pictures. In the background of the Mona Lisa, for example, you can see a blue, blurred landscape.

As well as aerial perspective, there is **linear perspective**. In it, things in the distance are drawn smaller and lines run towards a vanishing point. Both kinds can easily be combined. In Chinese landscape painting, too, distant mountains are often painted pale and delicate. If you paint a landscape yourself, you can easily try out aerial perspective.

gewusst: Without air, for example on the Moon, there is no aerial perspective: distant things look just as sharp there as near ones.
The same effect that makes distant mountains bluish also makes the sky blue.

teile.einleitung: If you are out and about in a strange town, you sometimes have to ask the way. With a few English expressions you will understand any directions.
wichtigste: “Turn left” means to go round the corner to the left, “turn right” to the right.
“Go straight on” means to keep going forward.
“Opposite” means facing, “next to” means beside.
A Kreuzung is a “crossroads”, a Kreisel a “roundabout”.
You ask politely: “Excuse me, how do I get to the station?”

abschnitte.text: You politely address strangers with **Excuse me**. Then you ask: “How do I get to the station?” The question needs “do” because it is in the simple present. You can also ask: “Where is the post office, please?”

**Turn left** means to go round to the left, **turn right** to the right. **Go straight on** or “go straight ahead” means to keep walking forward. “Take the second turning on the right” means: take the second road on the right. So you count the roads on the right-hand side.

**Opposite** means facing: “The bank is opposite the post office.” **Next to**, **behind** and **between** are useful too. “It's just around the corner” means that something is very close by. Then you have almost arrived.

A Kreuzung is called a **crossroads**, in the USA often an “intersection”. A traffic light is called **traffic lights**. A **roundabout** is a junction where traffic goes round in a circle, usually called a “Kreisel” in Switzerland. By the way, in Great Britain people drive on the left, so when crossing the road there you look right first.

gewusst: In London many pedestrian crossings have “look right” written on the ground so that visitors look in the right direction.

teile.einleitung: Lime trees, also called lindens, are large broadleaved trees with heart-shaped leaves and fragrant flowers. Their wood is soft and even and is especially good for carving.
wichtigste: In Switzerland mainly the large-leaved lime and the small-leaved lime grow.
Lime leaves are heart-shaped.
In early summer the flowers smell strongly and attract lots of bees.
Tea is made from dried lime flowers.
Lime wood is soft, has fine fibres and hardly splinters.
That is why many wooden figures are carved from lime.

abschnitte.text: Lime trees can grow very large and live for several hundred years. Their **heart-shaped leaves** have toothed edges. In early summer they bloom with small, yellowish flowers that have a strong **scent**. Then the trees hum because lots of bees arrive. This produces lime blossom honey.

In the past people liked to plant lime trees in the middle of the village or in the square in front of the church. Under the **village lime tree** people met, held celebrations or had meetings. In some places courts were also held under a lime tree. That is why many streets and squares are called Lindenstrasse or Lindenplatz. In Switzerland, too, there are famous old lime trees that are protected.

**Lime wood** is pale, soft and very even. It has fine fibres and **hardly splinters**. That is why it can be worked in all directions with knives and carving chisels. Many nativity figures, masks and wooden figures are carved from lime. Famous sculptors of the Middle Ages, such as Tilman Riemenschneider, also created large altar figures from lime wood.

The flowers of the lime tree are collected in summer and dried. They are used to make **lime blossom tea**. It has a mild, slightly sweet taste. Many people like to drink it when they have a cold. But you should only collect flowers from trees that do not stand right next to busy roads.

gewusst: Because lime wood is so good for carving, it used to be called “saints’ wood”.
The fruits of the lime tree have a small wing-like leaf and spin like a propeller as they fall.

teile.einleitung: The Bauhaus was a school of design, art and architecture in Germany. It existed from 1919 to 1933 and changed the design of houses, furniture and everyday objects all over the world. Several Swiss people also played an important part in it.
wichtigste: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919.
The school moved to Dessau in 1925 and to Berlin in 1932.
In 1933 it closed under pressure from the Nazis.
The Basel architect Hannes Meyer led the Bauhaus from 1928 to 1930.
The Swiss artist Johannes Itten developed the preliminary course and a theory of colour.
Important principles were “Form follows function” and “Less is more”.

abschnitte.text: **Walter Gropius** founded the State **Bauhaus** in **Weimar** in 1919. The school wanted to bring **art and craft** together, and later **industry** too. The students learnt in workshops for wood, metal, weaving, ceramics and printing. Their designs were meant to be beautiful, practical and affordable for many people.

In 1925 the Bauhaus moved to **Dessau**, in 1932 to **Berlin**. In 1933 it closed under pressure from the **Nazis**. After Gropius, the **Basel architect Hannes Meyer** led the school from 1928 to 1930. He stressed social and practical questions. The last director was **Ludwig Mies van der Rohe**, who is associated with the motto **“Less is more”**.

All students first attended a **preliminary course**. It was developed by the Swiss painter **Johannes Itten** from the canton of Bern. There they practised with shapes, materials and colours. Itten's twelve-part **colour wheel** is still used in lessons today. **Paul Klee**, who grew up near Bern, and **Wassily Kandinsky** also taught at the Bauhaus.

In 1925 **Marcel Breuer** designed an armchair made of bent **steel tubing**. The idea came to him from the handlebars of his bicycle. The B3 chair was later called the **“Wassily”**. From 1927 **Gunta Stölzl**, the first woman to become a master there, led the **weaving workshop** and made it one of the most successful workshops. Later she lived and worked in Zurich.

The Bauhaus took up the principle **“Form follows function”**. It comes from the American architect **Louis Sullivan** and means: the shape of an object should come from its purpose. After the war the Swiss **Max Bill**, a former Bauhaus student, carried these ideas on. From 1953 he was the first rector of the **Ulm School of Design**.

gewusst: The Bauhaus sites in Weimar and Dessau have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996.
The Bauhaus existed for only 14 years, but it still shapes design today.

teile.einleitung: Safety at work means protecting yourself from injury when doing crafts and handiwork. In the workshop there are sharp tools, spinning machines and electricity. With a few simple rules, working stays safe.
wichtigste: When drilling and sanding you wear safety goggles.
Long hair is tied back before working at machines.
At spinning machines such as the pillar drill you do not wear gloves.
Small workpieces are clamped in a machine vice.
With a knife you always cut away from your body.
If a cable is damaged: pull out the plug, do not use it and report it.

abschnitte.text: When drilling, sanding and sawing, **shavings and dust** fly around. **Safety goggles** protect your eyes from them. With loud machines, **ear protection** helps. If there is a lot of dust, you wear a dust mask. You put on the right equipment before you switch the machine on.

On the **pillar drill**, the spindle with the drill bit turns very fast. Loose **long hair**, loose sleeves, scarves or jewellery can be caught and wound up. That is why you tie your hair back and wear close-fitting clothes. **Gloves** are also forbidden here, because they can get caught on the drill bit and pull your hand in.

When drilling, the drill bit can **catch** in the material. Then it spins the workpiece round. So you never hold a small workpiece by hand, but clamp it in a **machine vice**. That way it stays safely in place, and your hands are well away from the drill.

With a **craft knife** or a **carving knife** you always cut **away from your body**. If the knife slips, it slides into empty space instead of into your hand or leg. The hand holding the material stays **behind the blade**. After use you slide the blade of the craft knife back in.

A **damaged cable** can cause an electric shock. You then immediately pull out the plug, stop using the machine and report the damage to the teacher. Only a **qualified person** may repair it. A tidy workplace also helps to avoid accidents. In Switzerland **Suva** works to prevent accidents at work.

gewusst: Many accidents in the workshop are not caused by the machine itself but by untidiness or rushing.
Machines often have a clearly visible red emergency stop button.

teile.einleitung: A button is a small fastener on clothes. You push it through a buttonhole so that a shirt, a jacket or a pair of trousers stays closed.
wichtigste: Buttons keep clothes closed.
The button is pushed through the buttonhole.
Many flat buttons have two or four holes.
You sew a button on with a needle and thread.
A press stud consists of two parts and closes with a click.
Buttons are made of plastic, metal, wood, horn and other materials.
The zip is a different fastener with lots of little teeth.

abschnitte.text: The **buttonhole** is a narrow slit in the fabric. Its edge is sewn round with lots of small stitches so that it does not fray. The button is a little bigger than the hole when it lies flat. If you tilt it, it fits through and then holds firmly. Buttons with buttonholes spread in Europe in the Middle Ages.

Many flat buttons have **two or four holes**. Others have a small loop at the back; this is a **shank button**. It is sewn on through the loop, and you see no thread at the front. Buttons are made of **plastic**, metal, wood, horn or mother-of-pearl. Some are plain, others are little pieces of jewellery.

You thread a thread through the **needle** and tie a knot at the end. Then you push the needle several times through the holes of the button into the fabric and back again. With four holes you can sew crosswise or in parallel. Leave a little space between the button and the fabric so that the button can be done up easily. At the end you fasten off the thread well on the back.

A **press stud** has a top part and a bottom part. When you press them together, they snap shut with a click. In a **zip**, lots of little teeth lock into each other when you pull the slider. There are also Velcro fasteners, hooks and eyes. Which fastener is right depends on the piece of clothing.

gewusst: On men’s shirts the buttons are usually on the right side, on women’s blouses often on the left.
On machines, too, people talk about buttons, for example the lift button, even though it holds nothing closed.

teile.einleitung: Gestalt psychology studies how we perceive things as a whole. It began at the start of the 20th century and explains why we arrange single dots and lines into shapes and groups.
wichtigste: Gestalt psychology researches how we perceive shapes and wholes.
Max Wertheimer is seen as a co-founder of Gestalt psychology.
In 1923 he published basic studies on the Gestalt principles.
Other important researchers were Wolfgang Köhler and Kurt Koffka.
A well-known motto is: the whole is more than the sum of its parts.

abschnitte.text: When we look at a picture, we do not simply see lots of single dots. Our brain immediately arranges them into **gestalts**, that is, into shapes and groups. **Gestalt psychology** researches the rules by which this happens. It stresses that the **whole** has a different effect from its single parts. A melody, for example, stays recognisable even if you play it in a different key.

**Max Wertheimer** is seen as a co-founder of Gestalt psychology. Together with **Wolfgang Köhler** and **Kurt Koffka** he shaped this field of research. In 1923 his work “Investigations in Gestalt Theory” was published. In it he described how we arrange single elements into groups, for example by closeness or similarity. Today these rules are called **Gestalt principles**.

The findings of Gestalt psychology are used in **art**, **graphic design** and **advertising**. Anyone who designs a poster, a logo or a website arranges the elements so that people understand them quickly. This knowledge also helps with road signs and maps. In this way an old theory reaches right into our everyday lives.

gewusst: The German word “Gestalt” is also used in English as a technical term.

teile.einleitung: Cotton is one of the most important natural fibres in the world. It comes from the cotton plant and is made into yarn and fabric. T-shirts, jeans and towels, for example, are made of cotton.
wichtigste: Cotton fibres are the seed hairs of the cotton plant.
The fibres grow in a seed capsule, the boll, which bursts open when ripe.
Cotton consists almost entirely of cellulose.
It is very absorbent and therefore good for towels.
Cotton grows in warm areas and needs a lot of water.
The fibres are spun into yarn and then woven or knitted.

abschnitte.text: The **cotton plant** belongs to the **mallow family** and grows in warm countries. After flowering it forms a **seed capsule**, the boll. Inside are the seeds, on which fine white **seed hairs** grow. When the boll is ripe, it bursts open and the fluffy fibre spills out. These hairs are the cotton fibres.

After the **harvest** the fibres are separated from the seeds. Then they are cleaned and combed. In **spinning**, many short fibres are twisted into a long, strong **yarn**. The yarn is made into fabric by **weaving** or **knitting**. It can be dyed or printed.

Cotton consists almost entirely of **cellulose**. It is very **absorbent** and can take up a lot of moisture. That is why cotton **towels** dry you well. Cotton is kind to the skin, soft and easy to wash. But it dries more slowly than many synthetic fibres and can crease.

Cotton is grown in many countries, for example **India**, **China** and the **USA**. Growing it needs a lot of **water** and often pesticides. With **organic cotton**, chemical sprays are not used. Anyone who wears clothes for a long time or passes them on saves raw materials.

No cotton grows in Switzerland. Even so, processing it was very important for a long time. In the 18th and 19th centuries many people in **eastern Switzerland** and the **canton of Zurich** spun and wove cotton, first at home, later in **spinning mills** and factories. In the canton of **Glarus** cotton fabrics were printed.

gewusst: The German word for cotton, “Baumwolle”, originally means “wool that grows on trees”, although the plant is usually a shrub.
Jeans fabric, also called denim, is mostly made of cotton.

teile.einleitung: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian painter, inventor and researcher who lived about 500 years ago. He painted the “Mona Lisa” and “The Last Supper”, two of the most famous pictures in the world. At the same time he drew flying machines, bridges and the human body, and so was far ahead of his time.
wichtigste: Leonardo da Vinci was born in 1452 in Vinci near Florence in Italy and died in France in 1519.
The name “da Vinci” means “from Vinci”, a small place in Tuscany.
He was a painter, sculptor, inventor, engineer and natural scientist all at once.
He painted the “Mona Lisa” and the wall painting “The Last Supper” in Milan.
He often wrote in mirror writing in his notebooks.
He drew flying machines long before there were real aeroplanes.
He is often called a universal genius because he was interested in almost everything.

abschnitte.text: Leonardo was born on 15 April 1452 in or near the small town of **Vinci** in Tuscany. His father was a notary, his mother a simple country woman. As a teenager he went to **Florence** to the workshop of the artist Andrea del Verrocchio. There he learned painting, sculpture and a lot about technology.

From about 1482 Leonardo worked in **Milan** for Duke Ludovico Sforza. There, from about 1495 to 1498, he painted **“The Last Supper”** on the wall of the dining hall in the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie. The picture shows Jesus with his twelve disciples at the last meal, at the moment when he says that one of them will betray him. Because Leonardo painted on dry plaster using a new technique, the paint soon began to flake off.

From about 1503 Leonardo painted the **“Mona Lisa”** on a panel of poplar wood. He worked on the picture for many years and even took it with him when he moved to France. With **sfumato**, soft and smoky transitions, he created the famous mysterious smile. Today the picture hangs in the Louvre in Paris and is visited by millions of people every year.
