teile.einleitung: The Freitag bag is a bag made of used lorry tarpaulins, old car seat belts and bicycle inner tubes. The brothers Markus and Daniel Freitag invented it in Zurich in 1993.
wichtigste: Freitag bags are mainly made of used lorry tarpaulins.
The first bag was a courier bag for cycling.
Old car seat belts are used as shoulder straps.
Bicycle inner tubes protect the edges.
Every bag is one of a kind.
The Freitag shop in Zurich West is a tower made of shipping containers.

abschnitte.text: In 1993 the brothers **Markus and Daniel Freitag** were looking for a bag that could stand up to rain and sat well while cycling. They sewed their first **courier bag** from an old **lorry tarpaulin**. Tarpaulins like this are very tear-resistant and waterproof. Other people liked the bag too, and so a company was born in Zurich.

A classic Freitag bag is made of three recycled materials. The outer shell comes from a used **lorry tarpaulin**. Old car **seat belts** serve as shoulder straps. The edges are protected with old **bicycle inner tubes**. In this way things from the rubbish get a second life.

abschnitte.titel: Every bag one of a kind
abschnitte.text: Every lorry tarpaulin has a different print, different colours and its own signs of wear. When it is cut up, every piece looks different. That is why no Freitag bag is exactly like another. Many buyers choose their bag because of a special letter or pattern.

In **Zurich West**, Freitag sells its bags in a special building. The shop is a tower made of old **shipping containers** stacked on top of each other. Here, too, you can see the idea of **reuse**. From the top you have a view over the district and the railway tracks.

gewusst: Not a single new main material is needed for a Freitag bag: tarpaulin, belt and inner tube all come from the rubbish.
The Freitag bag is a well-known Swiss example of upcycling.

teile.einleitung: Cardboard is a thick, firm material made of fibres, similar to paper. You need it for boxes, packaging and lots of craft projects.
wichtigste: Like paper, cardboard is usually made from wood fibres or waste paper.
It is thicker, heavier and stiffer than paper.
Corrugated cardboard has a wavy layer inside between two smooth layers.
Parcel boxes and removal boxes are made from corrugated cardboard.
So that cardboard folds neatly, you score the fold line first.
In Switzerland cardboard is collected separately so that it can be recycled.

abschnitte.text: Paper, card and board are all made of **fibres** pressed into a sheet. The difference lies mainly in thickness and weight. Weight is measured in **grams per square metre**. The heavier a sheet is, the more likely it is to be called card or board. In Switzerland people almost always say “Karton” in everyday speech, in Germany often “Pappe”.

**Corrugated cardboard** has a wavy layer of paper in the middle. It is glued between two smooth layers. The waves act like little arches and make the material strong, even though it is light. There is also corrugated cardboard with two or three wavy layers for heavy loads. That is why many parcel boxes and boxes for moving house are made of corrugated cardboard.

Cardboard can be cut with scissors or a **craft knife**. With a craft knife you put a cutting mat underneath and guide the blade along a metal ruler. For neat edges you score the fold line first, for example with a **bone folder**. Then the cardboard bends exactly in the right place. You can glue cardboard with white glue, paste or hot glue.

Cardboard is easy to **recycle**. In the factory, old boxes are turned into new fibres and new cardboard. Many Swiss municipalities have their own collection for cardboard, separate from paper. You fold the boxes flat and tie them together. Dirty cardboard, for example with food leftovers on it, belongs in the rubbish instead.

gewusst: The wavy layer in corrugated cardboard is built rather like the arch of a bridge: it spreads the pressure.
Corrugated cardboard was first used in England in the 19th century for the inside lining of hats.

teile.einleitung: The Locarno Film Festival is one of the best-known film festivals in the world and takes place in Ticino. Every August, films from many countries are shown there for about ten days. The best film wins the Golden Leopard.
wichtigste: The festival has taken place every year since 1946 in Locarno on Lake Maggiore.
It lasts about ten days in August.
The main prize is called the **Golden Leopard**, in Italian “Pardo d’oro”.
The leopard is the emblem of the festival.
On the Piazza Grande, films are shown in the open air on a huge screen.
Locarno is especially known for young film-makers and daring films.

abschnitte.titel: A festival with a long history
abschnitte.text: The Locarno film festival was held for the first time in **1946**. This makes it one of the oldest film festivals in the world. Locarno is in the canton of **Ticino**, in the Italian-speaking part of Switzerland. Every August film-makers, experts and lots of visitors arrive. For the town the festival is one of the highlights of the year.

Most famous of all is the open-air cinema on the **Piazza Grande**, the big square in the old town. One of the largest open-air screens in Europe is put up there. In the evening thousands of people sit in the square and watch films together. The audience there also chooses its own prize, the audience award. When it rains, the screening sometimes moves to a hall.

In the **international competition**, new films compete against each other. A jury of experts watches them and decides. The best film wins the **Golden Leopard**. There are also other leopards, for example for best director or for actresses and actors. The leopard also appears on posters and in the festival’s logo.

Locarno shows many films that are new and unusual. Young directors often present their first works there. Some of them later became world-famous. There are also programmes with old films, short films and Swiss productions. In this way the festival is a meeting place for people who value film as **art**.

gewusst: Several thousand people can fit on the Piazza Grande for a screening.
The festival began in the same year as the famous festival in Cannes, namely 1946.

teile.einleitung: With light and dark, that is with light and shadow, artists make things look three-dimensional on a flat sheet. In painting this kind of design has its own name: chiaroscuro.
wichtigste: Chiaroscuro means light-dark.
A cast shadow falls onto another surface.
A form shadow lies on the object itself.
With hatching you draw shadows out of lines.
The shadow always falls away from the light source.
Rembrandt was a master of light and shadow.

abschnitte.text: **Chiaroscuro** is an Italian word and literally means “light-dark”. It refers to designing deliberately with **light and shadow**. Strong contrasts make bodies look **three-dimensional**, as if you could touch them. The Italian painter **Caravaggio** became famous for his dramatic lighting effects. His figures often glow out of an almost black background.

The **form shadow** lies on the object itself, on the side facing away from the light. It makes a ball or a cube look three-dimensional. The **cast shadow** falls away from the object onto another surface, such as the table or the wall. Shadows always fall on the side that points away from the light source. So if the light comes from the top left, an apple’s cast shadow lies on the right.

With a pencil you can draw shadows by **hatching**. You put lots of parallel lines close together. The closer the lines, the darker the area looks. If you lay a second layer of lines across them, you get **cross-hatching**. This makes the area darker without you having to press harder.

A **grey scale** is a row of boxes. They are evenly graded from **white** through many shades of grey to **black**. If you practise it, you learn to draw shading deliberately and finely. That way you can get soft transitions, for example on a round ball.

The Dutch painter **Rembrandt van Rijn** lived in the 17th century. Like Caravaggio, he became famous for his special **light in the dark**. His figures stand out brightly from dark rooms. Rembrandt also painted himself dozens of times, at every age. His **self-portraits** show how he grew older.

gewusst: Rembrandt’s famous painting “The Night Watch” actually shows a daytime scene; it only looked so gloomy because of varnish that had darkened over time.
Just one soft pencil is enough to draw a whole grey scale.

teile.einleitung: Glue joins two things firmly together without nails or screws. There are many kinds, from white glue for wood and glue sticks for paper to sticky tape.
wichtigste: White glue is good for gluing wood.
Glued parts have to be pressed together and left to dry.
The glue stick is clean and good for paper.
You can mix paste from flour and water.
Hot glue is very hot and can burn the skin.
A thin layer of glue is usually enough.
Sticky tape is a tape with one sticky side.

abschnitte.text: A glue has to be able to do two things. It has to stick well to the surface; this is called **adhesion**. And it has to hold firmly together within itself; this is called **cohesion**. Many glues are liquid at first and then become solid. This happens when water evaporates, when they cool down or when a chemical process takes place.

**White glue** is a water-based wood glue. It is white and becomes almost transparent as it dries. You press the parts firmly together, often with a **clamp**, and leave them to dry in peace. For paper, the **glue stick** is suitable; you twist it out like a lipstick. **Paste** made from flour and water or from a powder is used for papier-mâché and for wallpapering.

In a **hot glue gun**, a plastic glue stick is melted. The liquid glue comes out of the nozzle at the front and quickly becomes solid as it cools. It is so hot that you can burn yourself on it. So never touch the nozzle or the fresh glue. You put the gun on its stand and pull out the plug after you have finished.

**Sticky tape** is coated with glue on one side. You can tear it off and stick it on straight away without waiting. There is clear tape, masking tape and strong packing tape for parcels. **Superglue** sets in a few seconds and also sticks skin together. That is why it is not for small children and must be kept away from the eyes.

gewusst: As far back as the Stone Age, people glued things with birch tar, which they got from birch bark.
Too much glue does not make a joint stronger, it only makes the drying take longer.

teile.einleitung: Annual rings are the rings you see on the cross-section of a tree trunk. Each ring stands for one year of growth, so you can use them to tell the age of a tree.
wichtigste: You can tell the age of a tree from its annual rings.
Each annual ring stands for one year of growth.
A ring consists of a light and a dark part of wood.
The light wood grows in spring, the dark wood in summer and autumn.
Wide rings show good years, narrow rings difficult years.

abschnitte.text: In our climate a tree grows quickly in spring. It forms light, loose wood called **earlywood**. In summer and autumn it grows more slowly and forms darker, denser **latewood**. In winter growth stops. A light and a dark part together make one **annual ring**.

If you count the rings from the middle to the bark, you know the **age** of the tree. The rings reveal even more: wide rings show years of good growth. Narrow rings point to difficult years, for example with drought or cold. Using **dendrochronology**, researchers can even work out the age of old building timber from its annual rings.

gewusst: In the tropics, where there is no winter, many trees do not form clear annual rings.

teile.einleitung: With comparison you compare things: big, bigger, biggest. In English there are simple rules for this and some important exceptions.
wichtigste: Short adjectives are compared with -er and -est: tall, taller, tallest.
Long adjectives are compared with more and most.
A comparative is followed by “than”.
Equality is expressed with “as ... as”.
Good, bad, many and far are compared irregularly.

abschnitte.text: With short adjectives you add -er for the **comparative** and -est for the **superlative**: “small, smaller, smallest”. If there is a short vowel before the last consonant, the consonant is doubled: “big, bigger, biggest”. If the adjective ends in a consonant plus y, the y becomes i: “happy, happier, happiest”.

Long adjectives with three or more syllables do not get an ending. You put **more** and **most** in front: “beautiful, more beautiful, most beautiful”. This also applies to many two-syllable words such as “careful”.

Some common adjectives have forms of their own. **Good** becomes better and best. **Bad** becomes worse and worst. **Many** becomes more and most. For distances **far** becomes farther and farthest; there are also further and furthest. These forms have to be learnt by heart.

A comparative is followed by **than**: “The Matterhorn is higher than the Rigi.” The Matterhorn is around 4,478 metres high, the Rigi not even half as high. If two things are the same, you say **as ... as**: “Tom is as tall as his father.”

gewusst: In German people say “als”, in English “than”. This is a common mistake: “bigger as” is wrong.
The superlative usually comes with “the”: “the tallest boy in the class”.

teile.einleitung: Alphonse Mucha was a painter and graphic artist from Moravia, in today's Czech Republic. He became famous with his posters in Paris. His pictures with beautiful female figures, flowers and ornaments are seen as typical of Art Nouveau.
wichtigste: Alphonse Mucha lived from 1860 to 1939.
He was born in Moravia, which today belongs to the Czech Republic.
From 1894 he became famous with posters for the actress Sarah Bernhardt.
His poster for the play “Gismonda” had a narrow, tall format.
His ornamental pictures are seen as the essence of Art Nouveau.
Later he painted the “Slav Epic”, a series of 20 large paintings.

abschnitte.text: Mucha was working in **Paris** as an illustrator when, at the end of 1894, he received a commission: a poster for the play **“Gismonda”** starring the actress **Sarah Bernhardt**. The poster was narrow and very tall, almost life-size. It immediately stood out in the streets of Paris. Sarah Bernhardt was delighted and afterwards had Mucha design more posters for her theatre.

Mucha's pictures usually show a **female figure** with long, flowing hair. All around there are **flowers**, tendrils and round ornaments like a halo. The colours are delicate, the lines curved. This style was so well known that people in Paris spoke of the **“Style Mucha”**. It is regarded as the essence of **Art Nouveau**, known in German as Jugendstil.

Mucha did not only design theatre posters. He also designed **advertisements** for biscuits, chocolate and bicycles, as well as calendars, jewellery and book decorations. This brought art into people's everyday lives. After **Czechoslovakia** was founded in 1918, he designed stamps and banknotes for the new state.

His largest work was the **“Slav Epic”**. It consists of **20 huge paintings** about the history of the Slavic peoples. Mucha worked on it for almost twenty years and finished it in 1928. The pictures are so big that they fill whole walls. He gave them to the city of **Prague**.

gewusst: Because the Gismonda posters were so popular, they were sometimes secretly taken down from the walls in Paris.
There is a museum in Prague dedicated to Alphonse Mucha.

teile.einleitung: Irregular verbs do not form their past tenses with -ed. It is best to learn them in three forms: the basic form, the simple past and the past participle.
wichtigste: Irregular verbs are learnt in three forms.
The 3rd form, the participle, is needed, for example, in the present perfect.
write, wrote, written.
eat, ate, eaten and drive, drove, driven.
With put all three forms are the same: put, put, put.
think, thought, thought.

abschnitte.text: Every irregular verb has three forms. The first is the **basic form**, for example “write”. The second is the **simple past**: “wrote”. The third is the **past participle**: “written”. You need the third form with “have”, for example “I have written a letter”.

Many verbs change twice: **eat, ate, eaten** or **drive, drove, driven**. In **swim, swam, swum** and **begin, began, begun** the vowel changes: the simple past has an a, the participle a u. “Written” is spelt with a double t.

With some verbs two forms are the same: **think, thought, thought**. “Thought” is pronounced roughly like “thawt”. With other verbs all three forms are even the same: **put, put, put**. “Cut” and “let” also belong to this group.

It is best to learn the forms aloud and always in threes. It helps to sort verbs into groups that behave similarly, for example swim, begin and drink. Many irregular verbs are very common, so practising them is worthwhile.

gewusst: Some irregular verbs are similar to German: “drink, drank, drunk” and “trinken, trank, getrunken”.

teile.einleitung: Art never comes into being in empty space, but always in a society with its ideas, powerful people, sponsors and conflicts. Art can praise, criticise, warn or make you think. Sometimes it is supported, sometimes banned, and sometimes it is even stolen.
wichtigste: Art and society influence each other.
Patronage means private support for art and culture; the German word Mäzenatentum is named after the Roman Gaius Maecenas.
In 1937 in Munich the Nazis mocked modern art in the exhibition “Degenerate Art”.
In 1939 the Galerie Fischer in Lucerne auctioned confiscated art from German museums.
Provenance research clarifies where works of art come from, for example when Nazi-looted art is suspected.
Picasso’s “Guernica” from 1937 is a famous picture against war.
Since 1985 the Guerrilla Girls have protested against the disadvantages faced by women in art.

abschnitte.text: Artists need money, materials and commissions. In the past, churches, kings and rich families such as the Medici in Florence were the most important clients. The German word for **patronage**, Mäzenatentum, goes back to the Roman Gaius Maecenas, who supported poets such as Virgil and Horace. In Switzerland today, culture is supported, for example, by the foundation **Pro Helvetia**, cantons, municipalities and private foundations.

Art can draw attention to injustice. In 1937 Pablo Picasso painted **“Guernica”** in response to the bombing of a Basque town in the Spanish Civil War. Since 1985 the anonymous group **Guerrilla Girls** have appeared in gorilla masks and use posters to show how few works by women hang in museums. Street artists such as Banksy also use walls in cities for messages.

The Nazis rejected modern art and confiscated thousands of works from German museums. In 1937 in Munich they showed the exhibition **“Degenerate Art”** to make fun of pictures by artists such as Kirchner, Marc or Klee. Many artists had to flee or were no longer allowed to work. In 1939 the **Galerie Fischer** in Lucerne auctioned part of the confiscated art.

During the Nazi period, many works of art were stolen from or forced out of the hands of their owners, above all Jewish owners. **Provenance research** looks into who used to own a work and how it changed hands. In 2014 the Kunstmuseum Bern inherited the **Gurlitt collection**, which sparked a wide debate. The Emil Bührle collection, shown since 2021 in the extension of the Kunsthaus Zürich, is also critically discussed because of where it came from.

With the sentence “Every human being is an artist”, the German artist **Joseph Beuys** meant that everyone can help shape society. He called this idea **social sculpture**. From 1982 he had 7,000 oaks planted in Kassel, each with a basalt stone beside it. Today many museums want to reach everyone, for example with programmes for children and free admission days.

Switzerland is an important place for the art trade. Since 1970 **Art Basel** has taken place in Basel every year, one of the most important art fairs in the world. At the same time Switzerland has to come to terms with its role in the art trade during the Nazi period. For this, museums today increasingly work openly with experts and with descendants of the former owners.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who supports art and culture with their own money.
The origin and ownership history of a work of art.
Works of art that were wrongfully taken from their owners.
Joseph Beuys’s idea that all people shape society like a work of art.

gewusst: More than two million people visited the exhibition “Degenerate Art”, far more than a simultaneous exhibition of art praised by the Nazis.
The German word Mäzen, meaning patron, comes directly from the name Maecenas, who lived more than 2,000 years ago.
The Guerrilla Girls still keep their real names secret and name themselves after dead women artists.

teile.einleitung: In additive colour mixing, coloured lights are laid on top of each other. The colours add up and become brighter. This is how every screen produces all its colours from just three primary colours.
wichtigste: The primary colours of additive mixing are red, green and blue, RGB for short.
Red and green make yellow.
Red and blue make magenta; green and blue make cyan.
All three colours of light together make white.
No light means black.
Screens, mobile phones and projectors mix colours additively.

abschnitte.text: In **additive colour mixing** you do not mix paint but **light**. If two coloured lamps shine on the same spot, their light adds up. That is why the mixed colour is brighter. The three **primary colours** are **red, green and blue**. If all three shine together equally strongly, **white** appears. Where there is no light at all, it stays **black**.

Each pair of primary colours makes a new colour. **Red and green** make **yellow**. **Red and blue** make **magenta**, a strong pink. **Green and blue** make **cyan**, a light turquoise blue. By changing the brightness of the individual lights, you can produce a great many different shades.

Every screen is made of tiny dots of light, the **pixels**. Each pixel has three even smaller dots that glow red, green and blue. Close up with a magnifying glass you can sometimes see them. From further away they merge into one colour in the eye. That is why computers are said to use the **RGB colour space**.

The human eye has three kinds of sensory cells for colour, the **cones**. They respond especially to reddish, greenish and bluish light. If the red and green cones are stimulated at the same time, the brain sees **yellow**. So additive mixing makes use of the way our eyes perceive colours.

With paints or printing inks, mixing works differently. This is called **subtractive colour mixing**: each colour swallows part of the light, and the mixture becomes darker. That is why printers use the primary colours **cyan, magenta and yellow**, usually with black added.

gewusst: If you mix red and green in a paintbox, you get a brownish grey, but with light you get yellow.
On a white area of a screen, all three colour dots glow brightly at the same time.

teile.einleitung: William Shakespeare is considered the most famous poet of the English language. His plays such as “Hamlet” or “Romeo and Juliet” are still performed all over the world today.
wichtigste: Shakespeare was baptised in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564 and died there in 1616.
In 1599 his company built the Globe Theatre in London.
From 1603 the company was called the King's Men.
His 154 sonnets were published in 1609.
In 1623 the first collected edition appeared, the First Folio.
He wrote most of his verse in blank verse.

abschnitte.text: **William Shakespeare** was baptised in April 1564 in **Stratford-upon-Avon** in Warwickshire. Later he went to London and became an actor and playwright. Towards the end of his life he returned to Stratford. He died there on 23 April 1616 and is buried in Holy Trinity Church.

Shakespeare's company of actors was first called the Lord Chamberlain's Men. In 1599 they built the **Globe Theatre** in Southwark on the south bank of the Thames. From 1603 the company was under the protection of King James I and was now called the **King's Men**. A faithful reconstruction of the Globe opened in 1997.

Shakespeare wrote comedies, tragedies and history plays. In **Hamlet** the Danish prince reflects on life and death in the famous speech “To be, or not to be”. **Romeo and Juliet** is set in Verona, where the Montague and Capulet families are enemies. Romeo is later banished to Mantua.

In his plays Shakespeare mostly uses **blank verse**, unrhymed lines with five stresses. In 1609 his **154 sonnets** were published. A Shakespearean sonnet has three groups of four lines and ends with a **rhyming pair**, the couplet. The rhyme scheme is abab cdcd efef gg.

After Shakespeare's death his fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell published the **First Folio** in 1623. It contains 36 plays. Without this first collected edition, about half of his plays would probably have been lost.

gewusst: The Spanish writer Miguel de Cervantes, author of “Don Quixote”, died in the same year as Shakespeare.
Many English expressions used in everyday life today come from Shakespeare's plays.

teile.einleitung: Lithography is an old printing process in which you print from a flat stone slab. It is based on a simple opposition: grease and water repel each other. Many famous posters of the 19th and early 20th centuries were printed this way.
wichtigste: Alois Senefelder invented lithography in 1798.
The name comes from Greek: “lithos” means stone, “graphein” means to write.
Lithography is planographic printing: the printing and non-printing areas are at the same level.
You draw with greasy chalk or ink on a smooth limestone.
The greasy areas take ink, the damp areas repel it.
Offset printing later developed from lithography.

abschnitte.titel: A stone as a printing plate
abschnitte.text: Alois Senefelder was looking for a cheap way to copy texts and music. In doing so he discovered that a special, fine-pored **limestone** is good for printing. Stones like this come mainly from Solnhofen in Bavaria. The stone slab is first ground smooth. Then the artist can draw directly on the stone.

You draw with **lithographic crayon** or ink that contains grease. Then the stone is treated chemically and dampened with water. The blank areas soak up the water, while the drawing stays greasy. If you now roll greasy printing ink over it, it only sticks to the drawing. The paper is laid on the stone and pressed down in a press.

With **colour lithography** it was possible to print colourful pictures. You needed a separate stone for each colour, and the colours were printed exactly on top of each other. This is how colourful advertising posters were made in the 19th century. Well known, for example, are the posters by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec in Paris. Many old Swiss posters for travel and tourism were also printed by lithography.

Stones are heavy and take up a lot of space. That is why they were later replaced by thin metal plates. This led to **offset printing**, in which the ink first goes onto a rubber blanket and then onto the paper. It is still based on the same principle of grease and water. Today magazines, books and brochures are often produced by offset printing.

Many artists still use lithography today. They like the fact that you can draw on the stone almost as with a pencil. This makes it possible to print fine lines and soft shading. A single print is also called a **lithograph**. The sheets are often numbered and signed by the artist.

gewusst: Senefelder discovered the process when he wrote notes on a stone and experimented with it.
Offset printing, which is used to print many books today, is a direct descendant of lithography.

teile.einleitung: The fretsaw is a fine hand saw with a thin blade held in a frame. You can use it to cut curves and figures out of thin wood. In handicraft lessons it is one of the most important tools.
wichtigste: The fretsaw consists of a frame, a handle and a thin saw blade.
When fitting the blade, the teeth point down towards the handle.
The saw cuts on the downward stroke.
The wood rests on a fretsaw table with a V-shaped cut-out.
You move the saw straight up and down.
On curves you turn the wood, not the saw.

abschnitte.text: The fretsaw has a metal **frame** that looks like a big U. The very thin **saw blade** is clamped between its ends. The **handle** is at the bottom. Because the blade is so narrow, you can saw tight curves with it. It is used mainly for thin wood such as **plywood**.

First you clamp the blade firmly at the top of the frame. The **teeth point down towards the handle**. Then you squeeze the frame together a little, for example against the edge of the table, and clamp the blade at the bottom. When you let go, the blade is pulled tight. A well-tensioned blade makes a high sound when you pluck it, and breaks less easily.

The **fretsaw table** is screwed firmly to the workbench. You lay the wood on it and saw in the **V-shaped cut-out**. The saw is held upright and moved evenly up and down, without pressing hard. On curves you slowly turn the workpiece. For a hole in the middle, you first drill a small hole, thread the blade through and clamp it in again.

abschnitte.titel: What you can make with it
abschnitte.text: With the fretsaw you can make animal figures, jigsaw puzzles, name signs or Christmas decorations. After sawing, you sand the edges smooth with **sandpaper**. Then you can paint or varnish the pieces. There are also electric machines that work like a fretsaw, the **scroll saws**. For beginners, though, the hand saw is ideal, because you can see clearly what is happening.

gewusst: Fretsaw blades come in different thicknesses, fine ones for thin wood and coarser ones for thicker wood.
A snapped blade is normal and happens to experienced people too.

teile.einleitung: Adrian Frutiger was a Swiss type designer from the canton of Bern. He designed some of the best-known typefaces of the 20th century. Many people read his letters every day without knowing it.
wichtigste: Adrian Frutiger lived from 1928 to 2015.
He grew up in the Bernese Oberland and first trained as a typesetter.
In 1957 he presented the Univers type family with 21 styles.
For Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport he designed an easily legible typeface for the signs.
This typeface went on sale in 1976 under the name Frutiger.
A version of Frutiger is used on Swiss road signs.

abschnitte.text: Adrian Frutiger was born in 1928 in **Unterseen** near Interlaken. He did an apprenticeship as a **typesetter** and then attended the School of Applied Arts in Zurich. At the beginning of the 1950s he went to **Paris** and worked for the type foundry **Deberny & Peignot**. His first major typefaces were created there. He died in 2015 in Bremgarten near Bern.

In 1957 Frutiger presented **Univers**. It is a sans-serif typeface, without the little feet on the letters. What was special was that from the very beginning it had **21 matching styles**, from thin to bold and from narrow to wide. Frutiger organised them with a **numbering system** so that the styles could be told apart easily.

From 1968 Frutiger developed the signage system for the new **Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport**. The signs had to be quick to read from a distance and while walking past. That is why the letters have open, clear shapes. In 1976 this typeface went on sale under the name **Frutiger**. Today it is used all over the world for signs, hospitals and companies.

In Switzerland, too, you often come across his work. Many **road signs** use a version of Frutiger, **ASTRA-Frutiger**. Frutiger also designed the typeface **OCR-B**, which machines and people can read equally well, and later **Avenir**. He is considered one of the most important type designers in Switzerland.

gewusst: Frutiger's OCR-B typeface is found, for example, in the machine-readable line on many identity documents.
The name “Univers” was meant to show that the typeface could be used in many languages and countries.

teile.einleitung: Art history tells how people have created pictures, figures and buildings over tens of thousands of years. It stretches from the animal pictures in Stone Age caves to today’s Pop Art and street art. Art history is also a science that researches, organises and explains works of art.
wichtigste: Art history describes how art developed from the Stone Age to today.
In the Lascaux cave in France there are famous Stone Age animal pictures.
The figure “Venus of Willendorf”, around 30,000 years old, was found in Austria.
You recognise Romanesque churches by thick walls and round arches; Gothic came after them.
A fresco is painted on still damp lime plaster, a mosaic is made of lots of little stones.
Neoclassicism around 1800 took ancient times as its model.
Andy Warhol became famous with pictures of soup tins.

abschnitte.text: People were creating art tens of thousands of years ago. In the **Lascaux cave** in France, discovered by teenagers in 1940, Stone Age people painted horses, deer and wild cattle on the walls. The **Venus of Willendorf** from Austria is a female figure of limestone only about 11 centimetres tall and around 30,000 years old. In Switzerland, too, Stone Age carvings were found in the Kesslerloch cave near Thayngen, for example a grazing reindeer.

The ancient Egyptians painted tombs and built pyramids and temples. The Greeks made statues with very natural bodies and temples with columns. The Romans decorated houses with wall paintings and **mosaics**, pictures made of lots of little stones. In Pompeii, which was buried by a volcano in AD 79, many **frescoes** have survived.

In the Middle Ages, art was mostly in the service of the Church. **Romanesque** builders made churches with thick walls, small windows and round arches. Then came **Gothic**, with pointed arches, tall towers and glowing glass windows. In monasteries, monks decorated manuscripts with coloured pictures and golden letters.

In the **Renaissance**, from about 1400, artists such as Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo rediscovered ancient times and explored perspective. Then came splendid Baroque, playful Rococo and, around 1800, **Neoclassicism**, which again took ancient times as its model. Romanticism stressed feeling and nature. In the 19th century the Impressionists painted light and moments.

In the 20th century art became more varied than ever before. Expressionism, Cubism, Dada and abstract art appeared. In 1931 the Spaniard **Salvador Dalí** painted melting clocks in the picture “The Persistence of Memory”, a major work of **Surrealism**. The American **Andy Warhol** made Pop Art famous with pictures of soup tins and stars.

Giorgio Vasari, who published biographies of artists in 1550, is seen as the founder of writing about art history. Today **art history** is a subject you can study at universities, for example in Basel, Bern, Zurich and Geneva. Art historians date works, research their meaning and work in museums. Important Swiss art historians were Jacob Burckhardt and Heinrich Wölfflin.

begriffe.erklaerung: Wall painting on fresh, still damp lime plaster.
A picture made of lots of small coloured stones or pieces of glass.
Art that shows dreamlike and unreal worlds.
Art that shows things from advertising, comics and everyday life.

gewusst: The original Lascaux cave is closed to visitors because the breath of so many people damaged the pictures; people visit an exact copy instead.
The Venus of Willendorf was found in 1908 during the building of a railway line.
Andy Warhol painted 32 pictures of soup tins, one for each flavour available at the time.

teile.einleitung: A centre punch is a pointed steel tool. You use it to knock a small dent into metal so that the drill afterwards starts in exactly the right place and does not slip.
wichtigste: The centre punch is made of hardened steel and has a cone-shaped tip.
You strike the back end with a hammer.
This makes a small dot, the **punch mark**.
This preparation is called **centre punching**.
The punch mark guides the tip of the drill and stops it slipping.

abschnitte.text: First you mark the place to drill on the metal, for example with a **scriber** and a ruler. Then you put the tip of the centre punch exactly on the point where the lines cross. The centre punch is held upright. A short, firm blow with the hammer makes the dent. Afterwards you check whether the dot really is in the right place.

Metal is hard and smooth. A drill cannot get a grip on it and **wanders**, which means it slides to the side. The punch mark is a small hollow that the tip of the drill fits into exactly. So the hole starts in the right place. For large holes, people often drill a pilot hole first with a small drill.

When centre punching, you put the workpiece on a firm, hard surface. You keep your fingers away from the striking face. When drilling afterwards, the piece of metal is clamped tightly and never just held in your hand. **Safety glasses** protect your eyes from metal shavings. There are also **automatic centre punches** with a spring that go off without a hammer.

gewusst: Lathes also have a “centre” point that supports a workpiece in the middle.

teile.einleitung: Shapes and lines are the building blocks of every picture. With circles, squares, triangles and different kinds of lines you can draw, design and even create whole works of art.
wichtigste: A circle has no corners at all.
A square has four sides of equal length and four right angles.
A zigzag line has sharp points, a wavy line is soft and round.
A spiral keeps turning around a centre point.
Vertical means from top to bottom, horizontal lies flat like the horizon.
The painter Wassily Kandinsky loved painting circles, triangles and lines.

abschnitte.text: The most important basic shapes are the **circle**, the **square**, the **rectangle** and the **triangle**. A circle curves all the way round and so has no corners. In a square all four sides are the same length and all corners are right angles. A triangle has three corners and three sides. You can draw almost anything from these simple shapes, for example a house from a square and a triangle.

Lines can look very different. A **zigzag line** goes up and down like pointed mountains. A **wavy line** swings gently like water. A **spiral** turns inwards like a snail shell. If you put lots of dots one after another, you get a **dotted line**.

A **vertical** line goes straight from top to bottom, like a flagpole. A **horizontal** line lies flat like the horizon. Lines that slant are called **slanted** lines or diagonals. Horizontal lines often look calm, slanted lines look more full of movement. Artists use this to show moods.

The painter **Wassily Kandinsky** came from Russia and lived from 1866 to 1944. He is seen as a pioneer of **abstract art**. Abstract pictures do not show objects, but shapes, colours and lines. Kandinsky also taught at the **Bauhaus**, a famous art school in Germany. His pictures with colourful circles and triangles are known all over the world.

gewusst: Kandinsky wrote a book called “Point and Line to Plane”.
Strictly speaking, every line is made up of countless dots.

teile.einleitung: Linen is a fabric made from the fibres of the flax plant. It is one of the oldest textiles of humankind. Linen is strong, absorbs moisture well and feels cool.
wichtigste: Linen is obtained from the stem fibres of **flax**.
Flax is a plant with small blue flowers.
Linseed oil is also obtained from its seeds.
Linen is strong, tear-resistant and feels cool.
A disadvantage: linen creases easily.
People were already making linen in the New Stone Age, in Switzerland too.

abschnitte.text: **Flax** is a slender plant with small **blue flowers**. Its stem contains long, strong fibres. From the seeds, called linseed, people press **linseed oil**. Linseed oil is used for cooking, for oil paints and for protecting wood. In the past flax was grown in many parts of Europe, in Switzerland too.

The plants are pulled out of the ground with their roots. Then they are left lying in the field so that the fibres come away from the woody part. This step is called **retting**. Then the stem is broken and the woody parts are beaten out. With a **hackle**, a kind of comb, the fibres are combed before they are spun into yarn.

Linen is one of the oldest woven fabrics. In Switzerland, fabrics and threads made of flax from the New Stone Age were found in the remains of **lakeside pile dwellings**. In ancient Egypt, mummies were wrapped in fine linen cloths. In the Middle Ages linen was an important trading fabric. Eastern Switzerland, especially the area around St Gallen, was known for its linen cloth.

Linen absorbs moisture well and releases it again quickly. That is why it feels **cool** in summer. The fabric is very strong and lasts a long time. However, linen **creases** easily. It is used for summer clothes, tablecloths, tea towels and bed linen.

gewusst: The German word “Leinwand”, meaning canvas, comes from linen. Artists still paint their pictures on stretched linen fabric today.
The words line and linoleum are also connected with the Latin name for flax, “linum”.

teile.einleitung: Cubism is an art movement that began in Paris from 1907 and completely changed painting. The artists broke objects and people down into angular shapes and showed them from several angles at once. A face can therefore be seen from the front and from the side at the same time.
wichtigste: Cubism began in Paris from about 1907.
Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque are seen as its founders.
The name comes from the French word “cube”.
Picasso’s picture “Les Demoiselles d’Avignon” from 1907 is seen as the beginning of Cubism.
Cubist pictures show an object from several angles at once.
A distinction is made between Analytical and Synthetic Cubism.
Collage was also invented in Cubism.

abschnitte.text: In **Cubism**, things are broken down into cubes, cones, flat surfaces and edges. Instead of showing an object from only one side, the artists painted several **views** side by side at the same time. So the picture shows more than you could see from one standpoint. The colours were often muted, mostly brown, grey and ochre.

In 1907 **Pablo Picasso** painted “Les Demoiselles d’Avignon” in Paris, a large picture of five women made of angular shapes. Many friends were shocked at the time. His friend **Georges Braque** painted landscapes in 1908 that seemed to be made of little cubes. A critic therefore spoke of “cubes”, and that is where the name Cubism came from.

In the early phase, **Analytical Cubism** from about 1909 to 1912, objects were broken down into many separate parts. Violins, glasses, bottles and people dissolved into lots of small facets. Picasso and Braque worked together so closely that their pictures could hardly be told apart. Sometimes the subjects can hardly be recognised any more.

From about 1912 the artists built up their pictures again from larger, clearer shapes; this is called **Synthetic Cubism**. Now they also glued newspaper, wallpaper, fabric or imitation wood onto the picture. This technique is called **collage**, after the French word for gluing. In 1912 Picasso created one of the first collages with a still life with chair caning.

Alongside Picasso and Braque, the Spaniard **Juan Gris** was an important Cubist and painted clear, colourful still lifes. Fernand Léger and Robert Delaunay also developed the style further. An important model was the painter **Paul Cézanne**, who wanted to break nature down into simple basic shapes. With the First World War from 1914, the joint work ended because Braque became a soldier.

Cubism opened the way to abstract art, which shows no objects at all any more. It influenced painting, sculpture, fashion and architecture. The Swiss architect **Le Corbusier**, together with Amédée Ozenfant, developed Purism as a response to Cubism. The **Kunstmuseum Basel** owns an important collection of works by Picasso and other Cubists.

begriffe.erklaerung: Latin for cube.
A picture in which paper, fabric or other materials are glued on.
The angle from which you look at or show something.
Art that no longer shows any recognisable objects.

gewusst: In 1967 the people of Basel voted in favour of buying two Picasso pictures, after which Picasso gave the city four more works.
For years Picasso hardly showed “Les Demoiselles d’Avignon” to anyone; it was only exhibited in public in 1916.
Musical instruments such as guitars and violins were often painted in Cubism.

teile.einleitung: Helvetica is one of the best-known typefaces in the world. It was developed in Switzerland and first appeared in 1957 under the name Neue Haas Grotesk.
wichtigste: Helvetica appeared in 1957 as Neue Haas Grotesk.
Max Miedinger and Eduard Hoffmann developed it.
It was created for the Haas type foundry in Münchenstein near Basel.
In 1960 it was renamed Helvetica.
Helvetica is Latin and means “Swiss”.

abschnitte.text: **Max Miedinger** and **Eduard Hoffmann** developed the typeface in the 1950s. They worked for the **Haas type foundry** in **Münchenstein** near Basel. In 1957 the typeface came on the market as **Neue Haas Grotesk**. To sell it in other countries, a new name was chosen in 1960: **Helvetica**. The word is Latin and means “Swiss”.

Helvetica is a **sans serif typeface**. Serifs are little feet and strokes at the ends of letters, like the ones you know from newspaper typefaces. Sans serif typefaces are also called **grotesque**. Helvetica looks clear, calm and neutral. That is why it is well suited to signs, logos and posters.

In the middle of the 20th century, Swiss graphic design became world-famous. People speak of the **Swiss Style** or International Typographic Style. Typical features are clear grids, lots of empty space and sans serif typefaces. Helvetica fitted this style perfectly. Soon it was used all over the world for company logos and signs.

gewusst: In 2007 a whole documentary film was even made about Helvetica.
Many company logos all over the world are set in Helvetica.

teile.einleitung: Josef Müller-Brockmann was a Swiss graphic designer from Zurich. He is seen as one of the most important figures of the “Swiss Style”, a clear and objective way of designing posters and printed matter.
wichtigste: Josef Müller-Brockmann lived from 1914 to 1996.
He worked in Zurich as a graphic designer and taught at the School of Applied Arts.
His concert posters for the Tonhalle Zürich from the 1950s onwards are famous.
He worked with grids, clear lines and typefaces without serifs.
In 1981 his book “Grid Systems in Graphic Design” was published.
His ideas are still used in layout and web design today.

abschnitte.text: In the middle of the 20th century, graphic designers in Zurich and Basel developed a very clear kind of design. It is called the **Swiss Style** or International Typographic Style. Typical features are typefaces without little feet, the **grotesque typefaces**, lots of empty space and strict order. Instead of decoration, information and readability are at the centre. Müller-Brockmann was one of the best-known figures of this movement.

Müller-Brockmann designed many concert posters for the **Tonhalle-Gesellschaft Zürich**. He did not draw musicians or instruments, but used circles, arcs and stripes. These **geometric shapes** are meant to make the rhythm and sound of the music visible. The lettering fits exactly into the order of the poster. Today museums show these posters as classics of graphic design.

A **design grid** is an invisible network of columns and rows. Texts, pictures and headings are lined up along these lines. This makes a page look calm and orderly, even when there is a lot on it. In his book from 1981, Müller-Brockmann explains step by step how to build grids like this. Newspapers, books, apps and websites still use the principle today.

Müller-Brockmann also passed on his knowledge as a **teacher**. Together with other Zurich designers, from 1958 he published the magazine “Neue Grafik”. It made the Swiss Style known in many countries. He also wrote books about the history of the poster and of visual communication.

gewusst: On many Tonhalle posters the music is shown only through shapes and colours, without any picture of an orchestra.
The grid principle from Müller-Brockmann’s book is built into many web design tools today.

teile.einleitung: Wood is a natural material from the trunks and branches of trees. It keeps growing back and is used for building, making things and heating.
wichtigste: On the cross-section of a trunk you can count the annual rings.
Each annual ring stands for roughly one year.
Most kinds of wood float on water.
You use sandpaper to make rough wooden edges smooth.
A splinter is a small, sharp sliver of wood.
The grain is the natural pattern in wood.

abschnitte.text: Wood comes from the **trunk** and branches of trees. On the outside, the **bark** wraps round the trunk like a skin and protects it from cold, animals and diseases. At the sawmill the trunk is sawn into long, flat **planks**. People use them to build shelves, boxes, furniture or floors. In Switzerland about a third of the land is covered with forest.

On the cross-section of a trunk you can see **annual rings**. A tree usually forms a new ring every year, so you can roughly work out its age. The lines on a plank are called the **grain**. It comes from the annual rings and the wood fibres, which is why every plank has its own pattern. A round, often dark spot in a plank is called a **knot**: that is where a branch once grew out of the trunk.

Most woods are lighter than water. That is why they float on top when they fall into water. So from early on people built **rafts** and **boats** out of wood. In the past, whole tree trunks were transported on rivers by tying them together and letting them drift. Only a few very heavy kinds of wood sink.

In handicraft lessons you saw, drill and sand wood. You make a rough edge smooth with **sandpaper**. It is coated with fine, hard grains. This also helps you avoid a **splinter**, a small, sharp sliver of wood that can stick into your skin. If you sand well, you get smooth and safe edges.

gewusst: Wood is a renewable raw material: where trees are cut down, new ones can grow.
The word “Spreissel” for a splinter is typical of Switzerland; in Germany people often say “Splitter”.

teile.einleitung: Industrial design shapes things that are made in large numbers in factories: lamps, radios, chairs or toasters. Good design should be beautiful, practical and easy to use.
wichtigste: From 1907 Peter Behrens created one of the first complete corporate designs for AEG.
Dieter Rams coined the motto “Less, but better”.
Raymond Loewy coined the MAYA principle: Most Advanced Yet Acceptable.
In the 1930s many everyday appliances were given a streamlined shape.
Planned obsolescence deliberately shortens the life of products.
From 1924 the Phoebus cartel limited the life of light bulbs to 1,000 hours.

abschnitte.text: From 1907 **Peter Behrens** designed almost everything for the German company **AEG**: products, logo, advertising and even factory buildings. This produced one of the first complete **corporate designs**. That is a uniform look by which you recognise a company straight away. That is why Behrens is seen as a pioneer of industrial design.

In the 1930s the **streamlined shape** was very popular in the USA. It came from the aerodynamics of trains and aeroplanes. Soon toasters and pencil sharpeners were given this sleek shape too, as a sign of modernity. The designer **Raymond Loewy** coined the **MAYA** principle: “Most Advanced Yet Acceptable”. A product should be as advanced as possible, but still seem familiar enough.

**Dieter Rams** was chief designer at the company **Braun** for a long time. He stood for simple, functional design and set out **ten principles for good design**. His motto is “Less, but better”. In 1956 the radio and record player **SK 4** appeared, designed by Hans Gugelot and Dieter Rams. Because of its see-through Plexiglas lid, people called it “Snow White’s coffin”.

In **planned obsolescence**, the life of a product is deliberately shortened. It breaks sooner or is made to go out of date, so that you have to buy a new one. A well-known example is the **Phoebus cartel**. From 1924 big light bulb makers agreed on a life of **1,000 hours**, although longer would have been possible. Today many people demand products that last a long time and can be repaired.

A well-known example of Swiss design is the **Landi chair**. Hans Coray designed it in aluminium for the **1939 National Exhibition** in Zurich. The chair is light, stackable and weatherproof. It is still made today.

gewusst: The word “obsolescence” comes from the Latin “obsolescere” and means “to wear out” or “to go out of date”.
The Landi chair has lots of holes in the seat so that it is light and rainwater drains away.

teile.einleitung: English does not sound the same everywhere. Between London, Newcastle, New York and Singapore there are differences in pronunciation, words and spelling.
wichtigste: Received Pronunciation is the traditional standard pronunciation of southern England.
Cockney from London's East End is known for rhyming slang.
Noah Webster promoted American spellings such as “color”.
British “lorry” is “truck” in American English.
In rhotic varieties the r after vowels is pronounced.
Tok Pisin is an official language of Papua New Guinea.

abschnitte.text: **Received Pronunciation**, RP for short, was for a long time the prestige accent and closely linked with the BBC. Today only a few per cent of the population speak it. There are also many dialects. **Cockney** comes from London's East End. In **rhyming slang** a rhyme replaces the word that is meant: “apples and pears” stands for “stairs”.

In Newcastle upon Tyne in the north-east of England people speak **Geordie**. The dialect of Liverpool is called **Scouse**. These dialects differ clearly from the standard in pronunciation and in some words. In Scotland, Wales and Ireland English sounds different again.

The lexicographer **Noah Webster** published his “American Dictionary of the English Language” in 1828. He promoted simpler spellings such as “color” instead of “colour” or “center” instead of “centre”. Words differ too: a British “lorry” is an American “truck”.

An accent is called **rhotic** if the r after vowels is pronounced. In General American you hear the r in “car”. In non-rhotic RP it disappears. So you can often tell British and American English apart from a single word.

English has developed independently in many countries. In Singapore people informally speak **Singlish**, with influences from Malay, Hokkien and Tamil. **Tok Pisin** grew out of an English-based pidgin and is now an official language of Papua New Guinea. India, Australia and Nigeria also have their own forms of English.

gewusst: A “true Cockney” used to be someone born within earshot of the bells of the church of St Mary-le-Bow in London.
A creole language develops when a simple contact language, a pidgin, becomes children's first language.

teile.einleitung: Impressionism is an art movement that began in France around 1870. The painters wanted to capture light and the fleeting moment, the way you see something in a brief instant. Their pictures are made of many small, visible brushstrokes and look bright and lively.
wichtigste: Impressionism began in France in the second half of the 19th century.
It was named after Claude Monet’s picture “Impression, Sunrise”.
The Impressionists’ first joint exhibition took place in Paris in 1874.
Above all, the Impressionists wanted to capture light and the fleeting moment.
They often painted outdoors in nature; this is called plein air painting.
Claude Monet created a garden with a water lily pond at Giverny.
Edgar Degas especially often painted ballet dancers.

abschnitte.text: The word **impression** means the effect something has on you. The Impressionists did not paint every detail exactly, but the impression that light, colours and movement make in a moment. With quick, short **brushstrokes** they placed pure colours side by side. Close up you only see patches, but from a distance a glowing picture appears.

In the 19th century a strict academy in Paris decided which pictures were shown at the official **Salon**. Because the young painters were often rejected there, in 1874 they organised their own exhibition in the studio of the photographer Nadar. Monet’s picture “Impression, Sunrise” hung there, showing the port of Le Havre in the morning mist. A critic mockingly called the group **“Impressionists”**, and the name stuck.

The Impressionists went out with their easels into gardens, to rivers and to the sea. This **plein air painting** became easier because there were now oil paints in tubes that you could take with you. Monet painted the same subject, for example haystacks or Rouen Cathedral, at different times of day. In this way he showed how strongly **light** changes colours.

**Claude Monet** is seen as the leading figure and lived at Giverny from 1883, where he created his water lily pond and painted until his death in 1926. **Edgar Degas** painted ballet dancers, horse races and scenes from everyday life in Paris. Auguste Renoir showed cheerful people dancing, Alfred Sisley and Camille Pissarro painted landscapes. Berthe Morisot and the American Mary Cassatt also belonged to the group.

Georges Seurat developed **pointillism**, in which pictures are made of lots of small dots of colour. Painters such as Paul Cézanne, Vincent van Gogh and Paul Gauguin went beyond Impressionism; they are called Post-Impressionists. In Germany, **Max Liebermann** from Berlin is seen as the most important Impressionist. People also speak of Impressionism in music, for example with Claude Debussy.

The largest collection of Impressionist pictures is shown at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris. Monet’s “Impression, Sunrise” hangs in the **Musée Marmottan Monet**. In Switzerland you can see famous works in the Kunsthaus Zürich, at the Fondation Beyeler in Riehen near Basel and in other museums. Today the once mocked pictures are among the most popular and most expensive in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: French and English word for the effect or feeling something gives you.
Painting outdoors in nature instead of in the studio.
Painting technique in which a picture is made of lots of small dots of colour.
Large official art exhibition in Paris in the 19th century.

gewusst: Between 1874 and 1886 the Impressionists held eight joint exhibitions in all.
Monet painted around 250 pictures of water lilies.
The metal paint tube was invented in 1841 and made painting outdoors much easier.

teile.einleitung: Linocut is a printing technique in which you cut a picture into a sheet of linoleum. The areas left standing take up ink and are printed onto paper. In this way you can print a picture many times.
wichtigste: Linocut is a **relief printing** process.
Only the raised areas take up ink and print.
Whatever you cut away stays white in the print.
The print is the mirror image of the block, so lettering must be cut back to front.
You cut with **gouges** and apply the ink with a rubber roller.
You always keep your free hand behind the direction of the cut.
In the reduction method, you keep cutting the same block for each colour.

abschnitte.text: In **relief printing**, only what stands up prints. You know this from a rubber stamp: the raised shape gets ink, the hollows do not. The **woodcut** is also a relief print. In linocut, you cut away everything that is meant to stay white in the print. So when planning, you have to think the other way round and consider what should be light and what dark.

When you put the paper on the block and print, you get a **mirror image**. With pictures you often do not notice this. With **lettering** you do: a word written normally would come out back to front in the print. That is why you draw lettering in mirror image on the block. One trick is to draw the design on tracing paper and lay it on upside down.

You cut with **gouges**, which have V-shaped or U-shaped blades. Narrow blades cut fine lines, wide ones remove large areas. The blades are very sharp. You always cut away from your body and keep the other hand **behind the blade**. A **bench hook**, against which you place the block, stops it from slipping.

The printing ink is rolled out thinly on a smooth surface with the **rubber roller**. Then you roll it evenly over the block. The ink only stays on the raised areas. Then you put a sheet of paper on top and rub it down firmly with a spoon or a baren, or you use a **printing press**. Peeled off carefully, the print is finished.

For a **print in several colours** there is a special way. First you print the lightest colour on all the sheets. Then you cut more parts out of the same block and print the next, darker colour on top. It goes on like this colour by colour. At the end the block is almost completely cut away and cannot be used again; that is why the process is also called the **reduction method** or “lost block”.

gewusst: Linoleum was invented in England in the 19th century as a floor covering. One of its ingredients is linseed oil, hence the name.
Pablo Picasso also created colour linocuts using the reduction method.

teile.einleitung: The hammer is one of the oldest and most important tools. It is mainly used for knocking in nails. There are many different hammers for different jobs.
wichtigste: A hammer is mainly used to knock in nails.
A hammer consists of a head and a handle.
The head is usually made of metal, the handle often of wood.
The claw of a claw hammer is used to pull nails out.
A rubber mallet or wooden mallet leaves no dents.

abschnitte.text: A hammer has two main parts: the **head** and the **handle**. The head is heavy and usually made of **metal**. The handle is often made of **wood** and is for holding. If you hold the handle far back, you can strike harder. If you hold it further forward, you strike more accurately.

Most often you need a hammer to knock **nails** into wood. First you tap carefully until the nail holds. Only then do you strike harder. While doing this, you take good care of your **fingers**. In handicraft lessons you learn how to use a hammer safely.

On a **claw hammer**, one side of the head is split and curved. With this **claw** you grip a bent nail and pull it out. A **wooden mallet** or **rubber mallet** has a soft head. With it you knock parts together without making dents or scratches. You need one, for example, when fitting wooden parts together.

As far back as the **Stone Age**, people used stones as hammers. Later they fixed the stone to a wooden handle, so they could strike much harder. Over time, hammer heads made of metal appeared. To this day joiners, carpenters and blacksmiths need their own hammers.

gewusst: A blacksmith shapes red-hot iron with a hammer on an anvil.
There is also a tiny bone in the ear called the hammer.

teile.einleitung: “To be” means “sein” and is one of the most important verbs in English. In the present tense it has three forms: am, is and are.
wichtigste: I am: ich bin.
He, she, it is: er, sie, es ist.
You, we, they are: du bist, wir sind, sie sind.
Short forms: I'm, you're, he's, we're.
The negative uses “not”: I am not.

abschnitte.text: With **I** you always need **am**: “I am Anna.” With **he, she and it** you need **is**: “He is ten years old.” With **you, we and they** you need **are**: “You are my friend.” or “We are in the garden.”

When speaking, people often shorten the forms. “I am” becomes **I'm**, “you are” becomes **you're**, “she is” becomes **she's**. The apostrophe goes where a letter is missing. Careful: “your” without an apostrophe means “dein” and is a different word.
For the negative you put **not** after the form of “be”: “I am not at home.” There are short forms here too: “I'm not”, “she isn't”, “we aren't”.
For a question you put the form of “be” at the beginning: “Are you hungry?” or “Is she your sister?” You answer briefly: “Yes, I am.” or “No, she isn't.”

gewusst: In English “you” means “du” as well as “ihr” and “Sie”, which is why it is always “you are”.

teile.einleitung: Autochrome was the first practical process for colour photography. The Lumière brothers from France brought it onto the market in 1907. For the first time, many people could take colour photographs.
wichtigste: Autochrome came onto the market in 1907.
It was invented by the brothers Auguste and Louis Lumière.
On the glass plate there were tiny dyed grains of potato starch.
The grains acted as colour filters in red-orange, green and blue-violet.
The result was a colour picture on glass, which was viewed with light shining through it.

abschnitte.text: The secret of the **autochrome plate** lies in tiny grains of **potato starch**. The grains were dyed in three colours: **red-orange, green and blue-violet**. They were mixed and spread in a thin layer on a **glass plate**. On top of this was a light-sensitive layer. The coloured grains acted like millions of tiny **colour filters**.

abschnitte.titel: A picture seen with light behind it
abschnitte.text: After developing, a coloured **glass picture** was produced. You looked at it by holding it up to the light or by projecting it onto a wall. Close up you can see the fine grains; from further away they merge in the eye into soft colours. Each autochrome was **unique**; it could not simply be copied.

Autochrome plates needed a lot of light. The **exposure time** was much longer than for black-and-white photos. That is why the people in the pictures had to keep still for a long time. Even so, the process was popular and was used until the 1930s. Then more modern colour films came along.

gewusst: The Lumière brothers are also regarded as the inventors of cinema.
Many autochrome pictures from before 1930 are the first colour photographs of the places they show.

teile.einleitung: Jean Tinguely was a Swiss artist who built moving machines out of scrap. His works turn, clatter and rattle. They count as kinetic art.
wichtigste: Jean Tinguely lived from 1925 to 1991.
He was born in Fribourg and grew up in Basel.
His machine sculptures belong to kinetic art.
The machine “Heureka” from Expo 1964 now stands at the Zürichhorn.
His Carnival Fountain from 1977 stands in Basel.
The Museum Tinguely in Basel was built by Mario Botta and opened in 1996.

abschnitte.text: The word **kinetic** comes from the Greek word for **movement**. So kinetic art is art in which the work moves. For this, **Jean Tinguely** built machines out of **scrap**, old wheels and motors. They turn, clatter and rattle, and some even destroy themselves. His machines are often playful and funny, but they also make you think about technology.

Jean Tinguely was born in **Fribourg** in 1925 and grew up in **Basel**. Later he lived and worked in **Paris** for a long time. There he became known for his machines. He often worked together with the artist **Niki de Saint Phalle**, to whom he was also married. Tinguely died in Bern in 1991.

For the **1964 National Exhibition** in Lausanne, Tinguely built the big machine **Heureka**. Today it stands at the **Zürichhorn** on the shore of Lake Zurich. At certain times it is switched on and moves. Then wheels and rods turn in a seemingly pointless but fascinating game.

In Basel, Tinguely’s **Carnival Fountain** from 1977 stands in front of the theatre. Its metal figures move and spray water. On the bank of the Rhine is the **Museum Tinguely**, designed by the Ticino architect **Mario Botta**. It opened in 1996 and shows the largest collection of Tinguely’s works. There you are allowed to set some of the machines going yourself.

gewusst: In 1960 Tinguely built a machine in New York that destroyed itself in front of an audience.
“Heureka” is Greek and means “I have found it”.

teile.einleitung: Figures of speech are language tricks that make texts livelier, more impressive or funnier. You find them in poems, speeches, advertising and everyday life.
wichtigste: Alliteration: words begin with the same sound.
Onomatopoeia imitates sounds, for example “buzz” or “splash”.
Hyperbole is a strong exaggeration.
Personification gives things human qualities.
A simile compares using “as” or “like”; a metaphor makes a direct equation.
Anaphora and chiasmus are popular devices in speeches.

abschnitte.text: In **alliteration**, words that follow each other begin with the same sound: “Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.” This is how tongue-twisters are made. In **onomatopoeia**, a word imitates a noise, for example “buzz”, “splash” or “sizzle”. In German it is called Lautmalerei, “sound painting”.

A **simile** is a comparison with “as” or “like”: “as brave as a lion”. A **metaphor** makes a direct equation: “He is a lion.” In **personification**, things are given human qualities: “The wind whispered through the trees.” After all, the wind cannot really whisper.

**Hyperbole** is a strong exaggeration: “I've told you a million times.” The opposite is **litotes**, an understatement using a negative: “It's not bad” for something very good. British English is famous for this kind of “understatement”. An **oxymoron** joins opposites, for example “deafening silence”.

In **anaphora**, the same expression is repeated at the beginning of sentences. In 1940 Winston Churchill said: “We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds.” In **chiasmus**, parts of a sentence are mirrored crosswise. John F. Kennedy said: “Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country.”

gewusst: Many figures of speech have Greek names: “hyperbole” originally means “excess”.
Advertising likes to use alliteration, because it is easier to remember.

teile.einleitung: Freitag is a company from Zurich that makes bags out of used lorry tarpaulins. It was founded in 1993 by the brothers Markus and Daniel Freitag and is a well-known Swiss example of upcycling.
wichtigste: The company Freitag comes from Zurich.
It was founded by the brothers Markus and Daniel Freitag.
In 1993 they sewed a first bicycle courier bag from an old lorry tarpaulin.
The bags are made from used lorry tarpaulins.
Freitag is a well-known example of upcycling.

abschnitte.text: The brothers **Markus and Daniel Freitag** were graphic designers in Zurich. They were looking for a tough, waterproof bag for cycling. Every day lorries rolled past their flat. So in 1993 they had the idea of sewing a **bicycle courier bag** from an old **lorry tarpaulin**. This idea turned into a company that today sells bags in many countries.

In **upcycling**, you turn rubbish into a new, valuable product. Freitag uses worn-out tarpaulins that would otherwise be thrown away. The tarpaulins are washed, cut to size and sewn. Because every tarpaulin has different colours, letters and signs of wear, every bag is **one of a kind**. For the shoulder straps the company uses old car seat belts.

In **Zurich West** there is an eye-catching shop belonging to the company. It is made of old **shipping containers** stacked on top of each other. This building also fits the idea of reuse. The container tower has become a well-known landmark of the district.

gewusst: The idea came about because the founders saw lorries driving past their window every day.
Two Freitag bags almost never look exactly the same.

teile.einleitung: Abstract art does not show people, landscapes or objects, but colours, shapes and lines. It came into being at the beginning of the 20th century and changed art for ever. Swiss artists also played an important part in it.
wichtigste: Abstract art does not depict visible reality.
It came into being around 1910 in Europe, with Wassily Kandinsky among others.
Kazimir Malevich exhibited the “Black Square” in 1915 and founded Suprematism.
Piet Mondrian painted with black, white, grey and red, yellow and blue.
The Zurich Concrete artists around Max Bill worked with mathematically ordered shapes.
In the USA, Action Painting and Colour Field painting developed after 1945.
The Swiss artist Sophie Taeuber-Arp was a pioneer of geometric abstraction.

abschnitte.text: The word **abstract** comes from the Latin “abstrahere”, to draw away. Abstract pictures break away from reality and show only colour, shape and line. They are meant to stir feelings or to show order and harmony. Around 1910 artists such as Wassily Kandinsky painted the first pictures with no recognisable objects.

The Russian artist Kazimir Malevich exhibited his “Black Square” in 1915. With it he founded **Suprematism**, an art made of simple geometric shapes. In the Netherlands Piet Mondrian and Theo van Doesburg founded the group **De Stijl** in 1917. Mondrian painted grids of black lines with areas of red, yellow and blue.

In 1930 Theo van Doesburg coined the term **concrete art** with the manifesto “Art Concret”. It means pictures that do not represent anything but consist only of themselves. In Zurich Max Bill, Richard Paul Lohse and Camille Graeser took up this idea and became known as the Zurich Concrete artists. Sophie Taeuber-Arp, born in Davos in 1889, was an early pioneer and was pictured on the former 50-franc note.

After the Second World War New York became the centre of art. Jackson Pollock laid huge canvases on the floor and let paint drip and pour onto them; this is called **Action Painting**. Mark Rothko painted large pictures with floating rectangles of colour, known as Colour Field painting. In Houston he designed a chapel that is now called the Rothko Chapel.

In the 1960s **Op Art** came into being, short for optical art. Artists such as Victor Vasarely and Bridget Riley painted patterns that seem to flicker or move. They made clever use of optical illusions. Pictures like these are found today in fashion and advertising too.

begriffe.erklaerung: Not representing objects, with no recognisable things.
A Russian art movement using simple geometric shapes.
Art made of colours and shapes that is not meant to depict anything.
Painting by dripping and pouring paint.
Art using optical illusions.

gewusst: The Swedish painter Hilma af Klint was already painting abstract pictures from 1906, but she hardly showed them to anyone.
Max Bill was not only a painter but also an architect, sculptor and designer of clocks and watches.
Under the black paint of Malevich's Black Square, researchers discovered older coloured layers of painting.

teile.einleitung: Art theory thinks about what art is, how it should be made and what makes it beautiful or important. Artists, philosophers and scholars have written books about this since ancient times. Their ideas have shaped how people painted, built and looked at art.
wichtigste: Art theory deals with the rules, aims and effects of art.
In 1435/36 Leon Battista Alberti described linear perspective for the first time in “De pictura”.
With his artists’ biographies of 1550, Giorgio Vasari is seen as the founder of writing about art history.
Johann Joachim Winckelmann praised Greek art with the words “noble simplicity and quiet grandeur”.
In 1915 Heinrich Wölfflin from Winterthur set out pairs of opposites such as “linear and painterly”.
Immanuel Kant described the beautiful as “disinterested pleasure”.
In 1911 Wassily Kandinsky wrote “Concerning the Spiritual in Art”.

abschnitte.text: **Art theory** asks questions such as: what is art? Should art imitate nature? What makes a picture beautiful? The ancient Greeks Plato and Aristotle already discussed whether art imitates reality; this is called **mimesis**. The study of beauty and perception is called **aesthetics**.

In the Renaissance, artists wanted to paint spaces the way the eye sees them. In 1435/36 **Leon Battista Alberti** described **linear perspective** for the first time in the treatise “De pictura”; in it all lines run towards one vanishing point. Since that time the **golden ratio**, with a ratio of about 1 to 1.618, has also been seen as especially harmonious. In 1550 Giorgio Vasari wrote biographies of famous artists in “Le Vite” and so founded the writing of art history.

In the 18th century **Johann Joachim Winckelmann** raved about Greek art and described it with the phrase “noble simplicity and quiet grandeur”. His ideas shaped Neoclassicism. In 1766 Gotthold Ephraim Lessing examined in his essay **“Laocoön”** how painting and poetry differ. A picture shows one moment, whereas a poem can tell a story that unfolds over time.

In 1790, in the “Critique of Judgement”, the philosopher **Immanuel Kant** defined the beautiful as “disinterested pleasure”. By this he meant that we like something without wanting to own or use it. In the 20th century **Walter Benjamin** wrote about art in the age of photography and film. He thought that a work loses its unique **aura** when it can be copied millions of times.

The art historian **Heinrich Wölfflin**, born in Winterthur, published the “Principles of Art History” in 1915. In it he compared Renaissance and Baroque using five pairs of opposites, for example “linear and painterly” or “plane and recession”. In 1911 **Wassily Kandinsky** wrote “Concerning the Spiritual in Art” and explained that colours and shapes affect the soul directly, like music. This essay helped to pave the way for abstract art.

Art theory helps you understand works of art better and talk about them. It provides terms with which you can compare and judge pictures. Many artists have written down their own ideas in **manifestos**, for example the Futurists in 1909. Today art theory also asks whether videos, actions or digital works are art.

begriffe.erklaerung: The study of beauty and perception.
Greek for the imitation of reality in art.
A way of drawing in which all lines run towards one vanishing point, creating depth.
A scholarly piece of writing about a subject.
A public statement in which a group sets out its aims.

gewusst: Even before Alberti, the master builder Filippo Brunelleschi carried out experiments on perspective in Florence using a mirror.
The Laocoön group, after which Lessing’s essay is named, is an ancient marble statue that was dug up in Rome in 1506.
Heinrich Wölfflin taught in Basel, Berlin, Munich and Zurich, among other places.

teile.einleitung: English is the language that most people around the world use to communicate. Most of them did not learn English as their first language, but as a foreign language.
wichtigste: According to Ethnologue (2026), English has the most speakers, about 1.5 billion.
Among native speakers, Mandarin Chinese is ahead.
English is today a lingua franca, a common language for communication.
The ICAO made English the language of international air traffic radio.
In Braj Kachru's model, Switzerland belongs to the Expanding Circle.
Globish and Basic English are simplified forms of English.

abschnitte.text: According to the language database **Ethnologue**, around 1.5 billion people speak English in 2026, counting first-language and foreign-language speakers together. Mandarin follows with almost 1.2 billion. Among **native speakers**, however, Mandarin is clearly ahead, with around a billion people. So most English speakers learnt English in addition to their own language.

A **lingua franca** is a shared language for people with different first languages. Today English plays this role in science, business and aviation. The **ICAO**, the UN's International Civil Aviation Organization, based in Montreal, requires pilots and air traffic controllers in international traffic to know English. English is strong on the internet too: in mid-2026, according to W3Techs, just under half of all websites had English content.

The linguist **Braj Kachru** divided countries into three circles. The **Inner Circle** includes countries where English is the main first language, such as Great Britain and the USA. The **Outer Circle** includes former colonies such as India, where English is an important second language. The **Expanding Circle** includes countries where English is learnt as a foreign language. Switzerland is one of them.

Again and again there have been ideas for a simpler English. In 1930 **Charles Kay Ogden** presented **Basic English** with only 850 basic words. He replaced many verbs with phrases using “get” or “put”. Later the Frenchman **Jean-Paul Nerrière** promoted **Globish** with around 1,500 words. The name combines “global” and “English”.

gewusst: In Switzerland English is not a national language, but it is learnt at school in every canton.
The share of English websites is slowly falling, because other languages are catching up on the internet.
